english: Tortoise the hero
ga: Akpokplonto ni ji Hiɛwalɔ lɛ
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Long, long ago, the wild animals ran out of water. They looked everywhere but found none.
ga: Be saŋŋ ni eho lɛ, nu efo koolooi lɛ adɛŋ. Amɛkwɛ he fɛɛ he shi amɛnaaa eko kwraa.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: They gathered to find a solution to their problem. All animals attended the meeting, except Jackal. Jackal said, “How can I attend a meeting with a stinking tortoise?”
ga: Amɛbua amɛhe naa koni amɛtao amɛnaagba lɛ naa tsabaa. Koolooi fɛɛ ba kpee lɛ, ja Osɔ pɛ. Osɔ kɛɛ akɛ, "Te mafee tɛŋŋ maya kpee kɛ akpokplonto ni shãa mɔ?"
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: At the meeting, the animals agreed to dig a well. Antelope said, “Our well will be deep and wide. When it is full, we will never run out of water again.”
ga: Yɛ kpee lɛ shishi lɛ, kooloi lɛ kpɛlɛ nɔ akɛ amɛbaatsa nubu. Adowa kɛɛ, "Wɔbu lɛ mli kwɔ ni elɛɛ hu, kɛ́ eyi lɛ, nu lɛ etãŋ wɔ dɔŋŋ."
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: They sang and danced as they took turns digging the well. Eventually, water broke through the ground and filled up the well. They were so happy. They had never tasted such sweet and fresh water.
ga: Amɛlá ni amɛjo be mli ni amɛtsakeɔ amɛhe kɛtsaa nubu lɛ. Yɛ naagbee lɛ, nu tsɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ mli ni eyi nubu lɛ mli obɔ. Amɛmii shɛ amɛhe waa. Amɛnako nu ni ŋɔɔ ni mli tse tamɔ nɛkɛ dã.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Then, one day, the animals realised that someone was swimming in the water and making it dirty. They took turns guarding the well.
ga: Kɛkɛ ni gbi ko lɛ, kooloi lɛ yɔse akɛ mɔ ko miiwu yɛ nu lɛ mli ni eewo mli muji. Amɛtsake amɛhe ni amɛbu nubu lɛ he.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Rabbit was on duty guarding the well. Jackal came along with his skipping rope. “What are you doing here?” asked Jackal. “Guarding our water,” replied Rabbit.
ga: Adaŋko yɛ nitsumɔ mli ni ebuɔ nubu lɛ he. Osɔ kɛ ekpãa ni ekɛfoɔ ŋwɛi lɛ ba. "Mɛni ofeɔ yɛ biɛ?" Osɔ bi lɛ. Adaŋko ha hetoo akɛ, "Wɔ nu lɛ he buu."
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Jackal asked Rabbit to play with him. The game involves a player being tied up with rope, closing their eyes and counting to a thousand. Rabbit agreed to play.
ga: Osɔ bi Adaŋko ni ekɛ lɛ ashwɛ. Shwɛmɔ lɛ biɔ ni akɛ kpã fĩ shwɛlɔ ko, ni amɛŋa amɛhiŋmɛii ni amɛkane kɛyashi akpe. Adaŋko kpɛlɛ nɔ akɛ ebaashwɛ.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Jackal tied up Rabbit, who closed his eyes and started counting. Jackal drank from the well and swam. Afterwards, Jackal took some water and left. Rabbit was still counting.
ga: Osɔ fi Adaŋko, ni eŋa ehiŋmɛii ni ebɔi kanemɔ. Osɔ nu nu kɛjɛ nubu lɛ mli ni efo nu. No sɛɛ lɛ, Osɔ ŋɔ nu ni eshi. No mli lɛ, Adaŋko miikane lolo.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Rabbit finished counting and opened his eyes. Jackal was nowhere to be found. Rabbit shouted for the other animals to come and untie him.
ga: Adaŋko lɛ gbe kanemɔ naa ni egbele ehiŋmɛii. Anaaa Osɔ yɛ he ko he ko. Adaŋko bolɔ etsɛ koolooi krokomɛi lɛ koni amɛbajie lɛ.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: The animals continued to take turns guarding the well, but all failed to catch Jackal. Tortoise said, “Let me keep watch.” He dived into the well to wait for Jackal.
ga: Koolooi lɛ tee nɔ amɛtsake amɛhe ni amɛbu nu bu lɛ he, shi amɛ fɛɛ amɛnyɛŋ amɛmɔmɔ Osɔ. Akpokplonto kɛɛ, "Ha makwɛ." Ekɛ ehe wo nubu lɛ mli koni emɛ Osɔ.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: When Jackal arrived, he thought, “There is no one here!” He began to drink. He felt something bite his tongue. Then, he was pulled under the water! The other animals came running when they heard Jackal crying and splashing.
ga: Beni Osɔ bashɛ jɛmɛ lɛ, esusu akɛ, "Mɔ ko mɔ ko bɛ biɛ!" Ebɔi dãa numɔ. Enu akɛ nɔ ko miimɔ elilɛi. Kɛkɛ ni, agbala lɛ kɛtee nu lɛ shishi! Koolooi krokomɛi lɛ jo foi kɛba beni amɛnu Osɔ yaafo kɛ ŋmɔlɔ.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: The animals tied up Jackal. Tortoise said to Jackal, “You wronged all of us. You will be punished.” The animals praised Tortoise as their hero. From that day, they enjoyed drinking clean water without any disturbance.
ga: Koolooi lɛ fĩ Osɔ. Akpokplonto kɛɛ Osɔ akɛ, "Ofee wɔ fɛɛ efɔŋ. Abaato bo toi." Koolooi lɛ jie Akpokplonto yi akɛ amɛhewalɛtsɛ. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ nɔ kɛbaa nɛɛ, amɛná he miishɛɛ akɛ amɛaanu nu ni mli tse ni nɔ ko nɔ ko gbaaa amɛnaa.
title: Tortoise the hero
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ntombifuthi Ncwayiba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Aku the Sun Maker
ga: Aku Hulu Feelɔ lɛ
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Long ago in a town called Sunland lived a girl with very long legs. Aku was her name. Aku wondered about a lot of things.
ga: Tsuutsu yɛ maŋ ko ni atsɛɔ lɛ Hulumaŋ lɛ nɔ lɛ, gbekɛ yoo ko kɛ naji kakadaŋŋ hi shi. Atsɛɔ gbekɛ nɛɛ Aku.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Sometimes Aku's father, Ataa Ankra, a fisherman let her go to the river with him to fish in his canoe. While Aku fished with her father, she wondered why the sun always looked at her from the sky. Sometimes Aku helped her mother, A'anua to cook. Aku wondered why palm oil looked red in calabash but yellow in yam pottage.
ga: Aku jwɛɔ nibii babaoo ahe. Be komɛi lɛ etsɛ, Ataa Ankra, wuolɛinyo ko, haa Aku kɛ lɛ yaa faa lɛ naa koni amɛya sha loo yɛ elɛlɛ lɛ mil. Beni Aku miisha loo lɛ, ejwɛɔ nɔ hewɔ ni hulu lɛ kwɛɔ lɛ yɛ ŋwɛi lɛ. Be komɛi lɛ, Aku waa enyɛ, A'anua, kɛ nihoomɔ. Aku jwɛɔ nɔ hewɔ ni mutsuru hiɛ tsuɔ yɛ tsene mli shi eyɛ wuɔfɔ su yɛ kpɔtɔmkpɔtɔ mli lɛ.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: And Aku wondered why Oti, her brother, and the other boys would not let her play football with them. Once, Aku asked the boys why. They only laughed and told her to go and play with the girls. The girls too would not play with Aku. "Your legs are too long," they always said. Aku was left lonely. She had no one to share her many thoughts with.
ga: Ni Aku jwɛɔ nɔ hewɔ ni Oti, enyɛminuu lɛ, kɛ gbekɛbii hii krokomɛi lɛ hãaa ni ekɛ amɛ atswa bɔɔlo. Be ko lɛ, Aku bi gbekɛbii hii lɛ nɔ hewɔ. Amɛ ŋmɔ lɛ kɛkɛ ni amɛkɛɛ lɛ akɛ ekɛ gbekɛbii yei lɛ ayashwɛ. Gbekɛbii yei lɛ tete taooo Aku kɛ shwɛmɔ. "Onaji kɛlɛ tsɔ," gbekɛbii yei lɛ kɛɔ daa. Aku he fee shoo. Enaaa mɔko ekɛ susu ejwɛŋmɔi babaoo lɛ ahe.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: But Aku soon became friends with the sun. She looked forward to seeing the sun every morning when she woke up. The cocks crowed to announce sunrise. Aku loved to dance in the early morning sun, her shadow dancing with her. The tweeting of birds made the cock crow music sweeter. The sun filled Aku with happiness and made her smile a lot. But one day, the sun did not rise.
ga: Shi Aku kɛ hulu lɛ babɔ naanyo. Daa leebi kɛji ete shi lɛ, ekpaa hulu lɛ gbɛ. Wuɔ gbɛɛmɔ shiɛɔ hulu lɛ shitee. Aku sumɔɔ ni ejo yɛ leebi maŋkpa hulu lɛ mli, be mli ni esusuma hu joɔ. Loofɔji agbɛɛmɔ lɛ haa wuɔ gbɛɛmɔ lala lɛ ŋɔɔ soro. Hulu lɛ hã Aku yi obɔ kɛ miishɛɛ. Hulu lɛ hã Aku ŋmɔ bibiibii babaoo.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Aku waited for the cocks to crow. They did not. The birds too did not tweet. And without the sun in Sunland, people could not go about their daily activities. Farmers could not go to tend their crops. The sky was grey and sad. Ataa Ankra could not go fishing. Children too could not prepare for school. And women could not go to the market to haggle over the prices of soap and kerosene. Aku missed all these. She missed the cock crows and bird tweets too. And she missed the sunrise more.
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, hulu lɛ eteee shi. Aku mɛ wuɔgbɛɛmɔ. Wuɔ ebooo. Loofɔji lɛ hu laaa. Ni kɛji hulu bɛ lɛ, Hulumaŋbii lɛ nyɛɛɛ amɛ daa kɛ daa nifeemɔi lɛ eko afee. Okwaafoi nyɛɛɛ amɛ ŋmɔji ashi amɛyasaa. Ni ŋwɛi fee lamulu su kɛ awerɛho. Ataa Ankra nyɛɛɛ faa mli looshamɔ eya. Gbekɛbii nyɛɛɛ amɛnaa amɛbua koni amɛya skul. Ni yei nyɛɛɛ jaji lɛ anɔ amɛya, kɛha samala kɛ grasin naa jarayeli. Aku shwe enɛmɛi fɛɛ. Aku shwe wuɔ kɛ loofɔji agbɛɛmɔ hu. Ni eshwe hulushitee lɛ po tsɔ.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Everyone wanted to know where the sun went. "Maybe the sun is dead," some people said. "The sun has travelled," said others. Aku disagreed, "No, the sun is not dead. And the sun has not travelled. Or it would have first told me." Some people chuckled at what Aku said. She continued anyway, "I tell the truth. The sun is my friend. The sun is not dead. It is only .." But no one would hear anymore. Everyone forgot about the sun. They laughed hard at Aku. The children laughed too. The children's laughter pained Aku the most.
ga: Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ tao ni ele he ni hulu lɛ etee. Mɛi komɛi kɛɛ, "Eko lɛ hulu lɛ egbo." Fã bii hu kɛɛ, "Hulu lɛ efã gbɛ." Aku kpãaa gbee ekɛɛ, "Daabi, hulu lɛ gboko. Hulu lɛ efãko gbɛ hu. Kulɛ ebaakɛɛ mi dã." Mɛi komɛi ye Aku wiemɔ lɛ he fɛo. Shi Aku tee nɔ ewie akɛ, "Anɔkwa. Minaanyo ji hulu lɛ. Egboko. E–" Shi mɔ fɛɛ mɔ kpa Aku toi boo. Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ hiɛ kpa hulu lɛ nɔ. Amɛŋmɔ Aku jogbaŋŋ. Gbekɛbii lɛ hu ŋmɔ. Gbekɛbii lɛ aŋmɔlɔ lɛ dɔ Aku fe fɛɛ.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Sad like the sky, Aku hastened into her house. On the way, she accidentally kicked her brother's football. The ball rolled into the kitchen. There was a calabash of palm oil in a corner of the kitchen. The ball hit the calabash. The calabash toppled. The palm oil in it spilled. The palm oil soiled the ball.
ga: Kɛ awerɛho tamɔ ŋwɛi lɛ nɔ lɛ, Aku sha ehe ebote eshia lɛ mli. Yɛ gbɛ lɛ nɔ lɛ, ejeee gbɛ ni enane tswa enyɛmi nuu lɛ bɔɔlo lɛ. Bɔɔlo lɛ kokro etee kpata lɛ shi. Tsene kɛ emli mutsuru ma kpata lɛ koŋ kome mli. Bɔɔlo lɛ tswa tsene lɛ. Tsene lɛ kpa. Mutsuru lɛ shwie. Mutsuru lɛ kpa bɔɔlo lɛ he.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Oti came into the house with one of his friends to fetch his ball. He saw the toppled calabash, the spilled palm oil and his soiled ball. Before he could run out to tell A'nua what Aku had done, Aku picked up the ball and ran off. The boys followed Aku. They all met A'anua outside the house. A'anua saw Aku holding the ball. Before she could call Aku and scold her, Aku ran past her. Oti, A'anua and all the people watched Aku run away. They wondered what she would do with a soiled ball.
ga: Oti kɛ enaanyo ko bote shia lɛ mli koni amɛyakɔ ebɔɔlo lɛ. Ena tsene ni ekpa lɛ, mutsuru ni eshwie lɛ. Ena ebɔɔlo ni ewu mutsuru lɛ hu. Dani eeejo foi ni eyakɛɛ A'nua nɔ ni Aku efee lɛ, Aku kɔ bɔɔlo lɛ ni ewo foi. Gbekɛbii hii lɛ nyiɛ Aku sɛɛ. Amɛ fɛɛ amɛ kɛ A'anua kpe yɛ agbo lɛ naa. A'nua na ni Aku hiɛ bɔɔlo lɛ. Dani eeetsɛ Aku ni ekã ehiɛ lɛ, Aku jo foi eho ehe. Oti, A'anua kɛ Hulumaŋbii lɛ fɛɛ kwɛ Aku yisɛɛ be mli ni Aku jo foi lɛ. Amɛ kpa amɛ yitsei amli nɔ ni Aku kɛ bɔɔlo ni ewu mutsuru lɛ yaafee.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Aku stopped when she got to the middle of the town square. She put the ball on the ground. With a mighty swing of her hands and a swift pull of one long leg behind the other, Aku kicked the ball. The ball turned round on the ground, spinning towards the edge of the town square. It hit the roots of the palm tree at one end of the town square.
ga: Aku wa edamɔ shi be mli ni eshɛ maŋ blohu lɛ teŋ tutuutu. Ekɛ bɔɔlo lɛ fɔ shikpɔŋŋ. Aku sha eniji kɛ naapkɛɛ hekãa, esha enane kakadaŋŋ kome fitirifitiri ema ekome sɛɛ, kɛkɛ ni etswa bɔɔlo lɛ. Bɔɔlo lɛ kokro ebɔle shi yɛ shikpɔŋŋ, ni eyi mli kɛ tee blohu lɛ koŋ afã. Bɔɔlo lɛ yatswa ŋme tso ni ma blohu lɛ afã lɛ fãji ashishi.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Then the ball shot into the sad sky. With mouths opened wide, the people of Sunland gazed after the flying ball. The ball flew beyond the clouds, beyond the gaze of the eyes. Everything was still. All was quiet. Suddenly, the sky cleared. The clouds became white, round and fluffy. Then a big ball came from behind the clouds. The ball was bright. And it was red and yellow like palm oil. The ball was the sun. Aku's sun. Everything stirred. The quietness left.
ga: Kɛkɛ ni bɔɔlo lɛ fã etee ŋwɛi tasuu lɛ mli. Amɛnaa ni ekpɛ amɛhe sɔŋŋ hewɔ lɛ Hulumaŋbii lɛ gbɛ amɛdaaŋ, be mli ni amɛkwɛ bɔɔlo lɛ yisɛɛ gãã kɛtee ŋwɛi shɔŋŋ. Bɔɔlo lɛ filiki eho atatui lɛ ahe, eho heni hiŋmɛi aaana. Nɔ fɛɛ nɔ shɔ. He fɛɛ he fee dioo. Trukaa lɛ, ŋwɛi tse. Atatui lɛ fee futaa, koklobii kɛ funyafunya. Kɛkɛ ni bɔɔlo wulu ko fã kpo kɛjɛ atatui lɛ asɛɛ. Bɔɔlo nɛɛ kpɛ haŋŋ. Bɔɔlo lɛ etsu ni eyɛ wuɔfɔ su tamɔ mutsuru pɛpɛɛpɛ. Bɔɔlo lɛ ji hulu lɛ. Aku hulu lɛ. Nɔ fɛɛ nɔ fɛne. Dioofeemɔ lɛ tee.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Soon, everyone was rushing home to prepare for their daily activities. Ataa Ankra looked for his fish bucket. Farmers took their hoes. Children bathed and dressed, ready to go to school. Women tied monies at the ends of their cover cloths. They carried their basins and baskets and hurried to the market.
ga: Be kukuoo sɛɛ lɛ, mɔ fɛɛ mɔ bɔi shiayaa kɛha gbi lɛ nifeemɔi agbɛjiianɔtoo. Ataa Ankra tao eloo goga lɛ. Okwaafoi kɔlɔ amɛ kɔii. Gbekɛbii ju amɛhe ni amɛsaa amɛhe, ni amɛfee skulyaa he kralo. Yei fimɔ kapɛji kpɔ yɛ amɛ nɔhaa mamai lɛ anaa. Amɛtere amɛ gagbai kɛ kɛŋtɛŋi lɛ ni amɛ sha amɛhe kɛtee jarayeli.
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: The sun returned to Sunland. Aku made it. A new day began...
ga: Hulu kusɛɛ eba Hulumaŋ. Aku ni fee. Gbi hee je shishi...
title: Aku the Sun Maker
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Idowu Abayomi Oluwasegun

english: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
ga: Ankamafio
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: In the busy city, far away from a caring life at home, lived a group of homeless boys. They welcomed each day just as it came. On one morning, the boys were packing their mats after sleeping on cold pavements. To chase away the cold they lit a fire. Among the group of boys was Magozwe. He was the youngest.
ga: Gbekɛbii hii kobɔlɔi komɛi hi shi yɛ Okaishi maŋ lɛ mli heko banee. Amɛbɛ ninaa ko kɛha nɔyaa, jetsɛremɔ gbɛ kɛkɛ amɛ kpaa. Leebi ko lɛ, oblahii nɛɛ miikota amɛ sai kɛjɛ kpo nɔ ŋanii lɛ, he ni amɛwɔ lɛ. Bɔ ni afee ni fɛi akaye amɛ fe nine lɛ, amɛsha jwɛi kɛfee kɔɔyɔɔ lɛ mli kulɔɔ. Gbekɛbii hii lɛ ateŋ mɔ kome ji Ankamafio. Lɛ ji gbekɛ kwraa ni yɔɔ amɛ teŋ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: When Magozwe's parents died, he was only five years old. He went to live with his uncle. This man did not care about the child. He did not give Magozwe enough food. He made the boy do a lot of hard work.
ga: Be ni Ankamafio fɔlɔi shi jeŋ lɛ, eye afi enumɔ pɛ. Ekɛ etsɛkwɛ yahi shi. Nuu nɛɛ kwɛɛɛ gbekɛ lɛ jogbaŋŋ. Ehaaa Ankamafio niyenii jogbaŋŋ. Ehani gbekɛ lɛ tsu nii deŋdeŋ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: If Magozwe complained or questioned, his uncle beat him. When Magozwe asked if he could go to school, his uncle beat him and said, "You're too stupid to learn anything." After three years of this treatment Magozwe ran away from his uncle. He started living on the street.
ga: Kɛji Ankamafio wie nitsumɔ lɛ he lɛ, etsɛkwɛ lɛ yiɔ lɛ. Be ni Ankamafio bi etsɛkwɛ lɛ kɛji ebaanyɛ eya skul lɛ, etsɛkwɛ lɛ yi lɛ ni ekɛɛ, "Olu tsɔ kɛha nɔ ko kasemɔ." Afii etɛ sɛɛ lɛ, Ankamafio nyɛɛɛ nyafimɔ nɛɛ dɔŋŋ hewɔ lɛ ejo foi kɛjɛ etsɛkwɛ lɛ ŋɔ. Eyabɔi gbɛjegbɛ lɛ nɔ hii.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Street life was difficult and most of the boys struggled daily just to get food. Sometimes they were arrested, sometimes they were beaten. When they were sick, there was no one to help. The boys survived from begging, and selling plastics and other recycling material.
ga: Gbɛjegbɛ lɛ nɔ shihilɛ wa naakpa. Gbekɛbii hii lɛ gboɔ deŋme dani amɛ naa niyenii. Bei komɛi lɛ amɔmɔɔ amɛ ni bei komɛi lɛ ayiɔ amɛ. Kɛji amɛheye lɛ, mɔ ko bɛ ni yeɔ buaa amɛ. Shika ni amɛnaa kɛjɛɔ nibaa mli kɛ nibii bibii hɔɔmɔ mli lɛ ni amɛkɛlɛɔ amɛ he. Kui krokomɛi ni miitao amɛye amɛ nɔ kɛ amɛbanɔɔ. Enɛ haa ni shihilɛ lɛ mli waa diɛŋtsɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: One day, Magozwe was looking through the garbage bins. He found an old tattered storybook. He cleaned the dirt from it and put it in his sack. Every day after that he would take out the book and look at the pictures. He did not know how to read the words.
ga: Gbi ko be ni Ankamafio miikwɛ jwɛi tsɛnsi lɛ mli lɛ, ena adesa wolo momo ko. Etsumɔ wolo lɛ he muji lɛ, ni ekɛ wolo lɛ wo ekotoku lɛ mli. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ, daa nɛɛ lɛ ekɔɔ wolo lɛ ni ekwɛɔ mfonii ni yɔɔ mli lɛ. Eleee bɔ ni akaneɔ emli wiemɔi lɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: The pictures told the story of a boy who grew up to be a pilot. Magozwe would daydream of being a pilot. Sometimes, he imagined that he was the boy in the story.
ga: Mfoniri lɛ wieɔ gbekɛ nuu ko ni ebatsɔ kɔɔyɔɔŋ lɛlɛ kudɔlɔ. Shwane fintiŋŋ po ankamafiolaa ni eji kɔɔyɔɔŋ lɛlɛ kudɔlɔ. Bei komɛi lɛ, enaa ehe akɛ lɛ ji gbekɛ nuu niyɔɔ adesa lɛ mli lɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: It was cold and Magozwe was standing on the road begging. A man walked up to him. "Hello, I'm Thomas. I work at a place where you can get something to eat," he said. Thomas pointed to a house nearby. "Do you want to go there to get some food?" he asked. Magozwe looked at the man, and then at the house. "Maybe," he said, and walked away.
ga: Je lɛ mli ejɔ ŋanii ni Ankamafio damɔ gbɛjegbɛ lɛ he eeba shika. Nuu ko nyiɛ banina lɛ ni ekɛɛ, "Helo, atsɛɔ mi Tɔmas, mitsuɔ nii yɛ biɛ nɔɔŋ, yɛ he ni obaana niyenii ni oye." Etsɔɔ lɛ shia ko ni asha he wuɔfɔ ni abu yiteŋ kɛ ziŋle bluu. "Miheɔ miyeɔ akɛ obaaya na niyenii yɛ jɛmɛ?" ekɛɛ. Ankamafio kwɛ nuu lɛ, ni ekwɛ shia lɛ, ni ekɛɛ, "Ekolɛ," kɛkɛ ni eho etee.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Over the months that followed, the homeless boys got used to seeing Thomas around. He liked to talk to people, especially people living on the streets. Thomas listened to the stories of people's lives. He was patient and respectful. Some of the boys started going to the yellow house to get food.
ga: Nyɔji babaoo sɛɛ lɛ, gbekɛbii hii kobɔlɔi nɛɛ bayɔse Tɔmas jogbaŋŋ. Esumɔɔ mɛi kɛwiemɔ, titri mɛi ni yɔɔ gbɛjegbɛ lɛ nɔ. Tɔmas bo mɛi awala mli saji toi. Ehiɛ ka shi ni eyɛ mɛi ahetsui, enyafiii mɔ ni ebuɔ mɔ. Gbekɛbii lɛ ekomɛi bɔi shia ni asha he wuɔfɔ kɛ bluu lɛ mli yaa kɛha amɛ shwane niyenii.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Magozwe was sitting on the pavement looking at his picture book when Thomas sat down next to him. "What is the story about?" asked Thomas. "I think it's about a boy who becomes a pilot," replied Magozwe. "What's the boy's name?" asked Thomas. "I don't know, I can't read," said Magozwe.
ga: Ankamafio ta shi eekwɛ mfoniri wolo lɛ mli kɛkɛ ni Tɔmas bata emasɛi. "Mɛni adesa lɛ kɛɔ?" Tɔmas bi lɛ. "Ekɔɔ gbekɛ nuu ko ni batsɔ etsɔ kɔɔyɔɔŋ lɛlɛ kudulɔ ko he," Ankamafio here lɛ nɔ. "Mɛni ji gbekɛ nuu lɛ gbɛi?" Tɔmas bi lɛ. "Mileee, mileee bɔ ni akaneɔ nii," Akamafio wie blɛoo.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: When they met, Magozwe began to tell his own story to Thomas. It was the story of his uncle and why he ran away. Thomas didn't talk a lot, and he didn't tell Magozwe what to do, but he always listened carefully.
ga: Be ni amɛkpe lɛ, Ankamafio bɔi lɛ diɛŋtsɛ ehe sane gbaa kɛtsɔɔ Tɔmas. Egba lɛ etsɛkwɛ lɛ he sane kɛ bɔ ni ejo foi kɛjɛ eŋɔ. Tɔmas ewieee tsɔ ni ekɛɛɛ Ankamafio nɔ ni efee hu shi ebo lɛ toi jogbaŋŋ. Bei komɛi lɛ amɛgbaa sane be ni amɛyeɔ nii yɛ shia ni akɛ ziŋle bluu ebu yiteŋ lɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Around Magozwe's tenth birthday, Thomas gave him a new storybook. It was a story about a village boy who grew up to be a famous soccer player. Thomas read that story to Magozwe many times, until one day he said, "I think it's time you went to school and learned to read. What do you think?" Thomas explained that he knew of a place where children could stay, and go to school.
ga: Be ni Ankamafio ye efɔmɔ gbijurɔ ni ji nyɔŋma lɛ, Tɔmas ha lɛ adesa wolo hee ko. Adesa ni yɔɔ wolo lɛ mli lɛ wieɔ akrowa gbekɛ nuu ko ni da ni ebatsɔ bɔɔlutswalɔ kpanaa ko he. Tɔmas kane adesa lɛ etsɔɔ Ankamafio bei saŋŋ kɛyashi gbi ko ni ekɛɛ, "Efeɔ mi akɛ eshɛ be ni obaaya skul ni oyakase bɔ ni akaneɔ nii. Te osusuɔ tɛŋŋ?" Tɔmas gbala mli akɛ ele he ko ni gbekɛbii baahi shi yɛ kɛya skul.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Magozwe thought about this new place, and about going to school. What if his uncle was right and he was too stupid to learn anything? What if they beat him at this new place? He was afraid. "Maybe it is better to stay living on the street," he thought.
ga: Ankamafio susu shihilɛhe nɛɛ kɛ skulyaa lɛ he. Esusu akɛ ekolɛ etsɛkwɛ lɛ sane ja akɛ elu tsɔ kɛha nɔ ko kasemɔ? Esusu akɛ ekolɛ abaayayi lɛ yɛ shihilɛhe hee nɛɛ? Eshe gbeyei. "Ekolɛ ebaahi kwraa akɛ mahi gbɛjegbɛ lɛ nɔ," ejwɛŋ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: He shared his fears with Thomas. Over time Thomas reassured Magozwe that life could be better at the new place.
ga: Ekɛɛ Tɔmas enaagba nɛɛ. Daa gbi lɛ nuu nɛɛ woɔ gbekɛ nuu nɛɛ hewalɛ akɛ shihilɛ yɛ shihilɛhe hee lɛ baahi fe he ni eyɔɔ lɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: And so Magozwe moved into a house and shared the room with two other boys. There were ten children living at that house. Along with Auntie Cissy and her husband, three dogs, a cat, and an old goat.
ga: Enɛ hewɔ lɛ Akamafio fa eyahi tsu ko mli yɛ shia ni abu yi eŋɔli lɛ. Ekɛ gbekɛbii enyɔ komɛi ni hi tsu lɛ mli. Gbekɛbii nyɔŋma ni yɔɔ shia lɛ mli. Kɛfata amɛ he lɛ, Nyɛkwɛ Sisi kɛ ewu, gbeei etɛ, alɔnte kome kɛ abotia momo ko hu hi shia lɛ mli.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Magozwe started school and it was difficult. He had a lot to catch up. Sometimes he wanted to give up. But he thought about the pilot and the soccer player in the storybooks. Like them, he did not give up.
ga: Ankamafio bɔi skul yaa. Nikasemɔ lɛ wa naakpa ejaakɛ nibii pii yɛ ni kpaako ebaakase. Bei komɛi lɛ enijiaŋ jeɔ wui. Shi esusuɔ kɔɔyɔɔŋ lɛlɛ kudɔlɔ kɛ bɔɔlotswalɔ lɛ ni ekane amɛ sane yɛ adesa wolo lɛ mli lɛ ahe. Tamɔ amɛ fee lɛ, lɛ hu enijiaŋ ejeee wui.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Magozwe was sitting in the yard at the house where he stayed, reading a storybook from school. Thomas came up and sat next to him. "What is the story about?" asked Thomas. "It's about a boy who becomes a teacher," replied Magozwe. "What's the boy's name?" asked Thomas. "His name is Magozwe," said Magozwe with a smile.
ga: Ankamafio ta yale lɛ mli yɛ shia ni abuyi eŋɔli lɛ mli eekane adesa wolo ni ekɛjɛ skul lɛ. Tɔmas bata emasɛi kpaakpa. "Mɛni adesa lɛ kɛɔ?" Tɔmas bi. "Ekɔɔ gbekɛ nuu ko ni batsɔ tsɔɔlɔ he," Ankamafio here nɔ. "Mɛni ji gbekɛ lɛ gbɛi?" Tɔmas bi. "Egbɛi ji Ankamafio," Ankamafio kɛɛ ni eŋmɔ mugɛɛ.
title: Magozwe (retold as Ankamafio)
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Lesley Koyi, Ga translation by Elizabeth Ocansey (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Wiehan de Jager

english: Ann interviews AI
ga: Ann bi AI saji
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "Hello and welcome to today's show, I'm your host, Ann Asante! Welcome to our viewers at home and here in our studio audience. Today, I have the guest everyone wants to interview. I'm so excited to interview today, Artificial Intelligence! Hello, AI. Thank you for coming to chat to us in the studio today," says Ann.
ga: "Miŋa bo ni mihere bo kɛba ŋmɛnɛ nifeemɔ lɛ mli, miji o-sanebimɔ he nitsulɔ, Ann Asante! Mihere bo kɛba wɔkwɛlɔi ni yɔɔ shia kɛ biɛ yɛ wɔ nitsumɔhe toibolɔi lɛ amli lɛ. Ŋmɛnɛ, miyɛ gbɔ ni mɔ fɛɛ mɔ miisumɔ ni ebi lɛ saji. Miyɛ miishɛɛ waa akɛ mabi mi saji ŋmɛnɛ, Jeŋ Nilee! Miŋa bo, AI. Oyiwaladɔŋŋ akɛ oba ni okɛ wɔ agba sane yɛ nitsumɔhe lɛ ŋmɛnɛ," Ann kɛɛ.
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "Thank you for interviewing me, Ann. Would you like me to use my audio to speak for the studio audience, and to show my replies on this screen?" asks AI. "Thanks, yes, using both your writing and speaking abilities will be helpful, AI," replies Ann. She adds, "Studio audience, a round of applause for AI, please."
ga: "Oyiwaladɔŋŋ akɛ obi mi saji, Ann. Ani obaasumɔ ni mikɛ mi-odio lɛ awie aha nitsumɔhe lɛ mli toibolɔi lɛ, ni mikɛ mihetooi lɛ atsɔɔ yɛ nɛkɛ skrin nɛɛ nɔ?" AI biɔ. "Shidaa, hɛɛ, kɛ okɛ oniŋmaa kɛ wiemɔ he nyɛmɔi fɛɛ tsu nii lɛ, ebaaye ebua bo, AI," Ann ha hetoo. Ekɛfata he akɛ, "Nitsumɔhe lɛ mli toibolɔi, ofainɛ, tswaa amɛdɛŋ kɛha AI."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "Let me get straight to the big question. Exactly, what or who is artificial intelligence?" asks Ann. She continues, "I know A.I. is a short form of 'artificial intelligence', and that it's a field of computer science. But who are you really, AI? We would like to get to know more about you."
ga: "Ha maya sanebimɔ wulu lɛ nɔ tɛ̃ɛ. Pɔtɛɛ, mɛni loo namɔ ji Jeŋ Nilee?" Ann biɔ. Etsa nɔ akɛ, "Mile akɛ A.I. ji 'Jeŋ Nilee' kuku, ni eji kɔmpiuta he nilee. Shi namɔ ji bo diɛŋtsɛ, AI? Wɔbaasumɔ ni wɔle ohe saji babaoo."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "I am ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence language program. I was created by computer software developers," responds Chat. Ann is confused, "What does all that mean?" "It means that I'm a type of AI that computer engineers made to communicate with humans. Different types of AI do different things. We don't all communicate like this," adds Chat.
ga: "Miji SanegbaaGPT, ni ji wiemɔ he gbɛjianɔtoo ko ni akɛ nilee ni akɛfee nii. Mɛi ni feɔ kɔmpiuta tsɔnei lɛ ji mɛi ni fee mi," Sanegba ha hetoo. Ann yiŋ efutu lɛ, "Mɛni ji nɔ ni enɛ fɛɛ tsɔɔ?" "Etsɔɔ akɛ miji AI henɔ ko ni kɔmpiuta he nilelɔi fee koni amɛkɛ adesai agba sane. AI henɔi srɔtoi feɔ nibii srɔtoi. Wɔ fɛɛ wɔwieee tamɔ nɛkɛ," Sanegba kɛfata he.
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "I know you can communicate, but what else do you do?" asks Ann. "My purpose is to help people. I am based on a complex language program. My program can understand and respond to a wide range of questions and subjects," replies Chat. "So, you're an artificial intelligence language program, and you help people," says Ann.
ga: "Mile akɛ obaanyɛ okɛ mɔ ko agba sane, shi mɛni ji nɔ kroko ni ofeɔ?" Ann biɔ. "Miyiŋtoo ji ni maye mabua mɛi. Midamɔ wiemɔ he gbɛjianɔtoo ko ni mli wa nɔ. Mi gbɛjianɔtoo lɛ baanyɛ anu sanebimɔi kɛ saji srɔtoi babaoo shishi ni eha hetoo," Sanegba haa hetoo. Ann kɛɛ akɛ, "No hewɔ lɛ, oji wiemɔ he gbɛjianɔtoo ko ni akɛ nilee ni akɛfee nii, ni oyeɔ obuaa mɛi."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "If you're such a clever program, there must be more you can do?" asks Ann. "Well, although I'm a machine, I can do many things that humans can do. For example, I can learn. I can look at information and learn patterns from it. I can learn to recognise different things, different faces, and even different handwriting."
ga: "Kɛ́ oji gbɛjianɔtoo ni yɔɔ ŋaa tamɔ nɛkɛ lɛ, esa akɛ nibii babaoo ahi ni obaanyɛ ofee?" Ann biɔ. "Ojogbaŋŋ, eyɛ mli akɛ tsɔne ji mi moŋ, shi manyɛ mafee nibii babaoo ni adesai baanyɛ afee. Nɔkwɛmɔnɔ, manyɛ makase nii. Manyɛ makwɛ saji ni makase nɔkwɛmɔnii kɛjɛ mli. Manyɛ makase bɔ ni ayɔseɔ nibii srɔtoi, hiɛi srɔtoi, kɛ nine nɔ niŋmaa srɔtoi po."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Chat continues, "I have learned lots of information created by humans. For example, I read lots of books, articles, websites, and social media." Ann asks, "Everything you know is based on information that people have written and produced?" Chat replies, "Yes, I train and learn using huge amounts of information (or data) created by humans."
ga: Sanegba tsa nɔ akɛ, "Mikase saji babaoo ni adesai fee. Nɔkwɛmɔnɔ, mikane woji babaoo, niŋmaai, wɛbsaiti, kɛ intanɛt nɔ kpeehe." Ann bi akɛ, "Nɔ fɛɛ nɔ ni ole lɛ damɔ saji ni gbɔmɛi eŋmala ni amɛfee lɛ nɔ?" Sanegba ha hetoo akɛ, "Hɛɛ, mitsɔseɔ ni mikaseɔ nii kɛtsɔ saji babaoo (loo saji nataamɔ) ni adesai fee lɛ nɔ."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "I can answer many types of questions faster than humans. I can solve very difficult problems that would take humans a long time to solve. I have more human knowledge than any single human. I can make decisions using the information I learn. I can help you to make choices, based on what I know about you."
ga: "Mibaanyɛ maha sanebimɔi srɔtoi babaoo ahetoo oya fe adesai. Manyɛ matsu naagbai ni wa waa ni baahe adesai be babaoo ni amɛtsu he nii lɛ ahe nii. Miyɛ adesa nilee babaoo fe adesa kome pɛ." "Manyɛ makpɛ miyiŋ kɛtsɔ saji ni mikaseɔ lɛ nɔ. Manyɛ maye mabua bo ni ohala, yɛ nɔ ni mile yɛ ohe lɛ naa."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Ann asks the audience, "Do we want computers to know everything that we know?" Then she asks Chat, "Tell me more about how computers learn about people?" Chat replies. "A computer has special tools that help me to collect information. But mainly, I learn from written information. I learn from all types of information that humans produce."
ga: Ann bi toibolɔi lɛ akɛ, "Ani wɔmiisumɔ ni kɔmpiutai ale nɔ fɛɛ nɔ ni wɔle?" Kɛkɛ ni ebi Sanegba akɛ, "Kɛɛmɔ mi bɔ ni kɔmpiutai kaseɔ gbɔmɛi ahe nii amɛhaa lɛ he saji babaoo?" Sanegba hetooi. "Kɔmpiuta yɛ nibii krɛdɛɛi ni yeɔ ebuaa mi ni mikɛbuaa saji anaa. Shi nɔ ni he hiaa fe fɛɛ lɛ, mikaseɔ nii kɛjɛɔ saji ni aŋmalaa mli. Mikaseɔ nii kɛjɛɔ saji srɔtoi fɛɛ ni adesai feɔ lɛ amli."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Chat continues, "I can read written and typed language. So far, English has been the main language I have used to get information. But, I have the ability to learn any language." Ann interrupts, "I understand that you know a lot of information. What about feelings? How do you feel about being an artificial intelligence?"
ga: Sanegba tsa nɔ akɛ, "Minyɛɔ mikaneɔ wiemɔi ni aŋmalaa kɛ wiemɔi ni aŋmalaa. Kɛbashi amrɔ nɛɛ, Blɔfo ji wiemɔ titri ni mikɛtsuɔ nii kɛnáa saji. Shi, miyɛ nyɛmɔ ni mikɛkaseɔ wiemɔ fɛɛ wiemɔ." Ann kpa ewiemɔ lɛ mli akɛ, "Minuɔ shishi akɛ ole saji babaoo. Ni henumɔi hu? Te onuɔ he ohaa tɛŋŋ yɛ nilee ni afee lɛ diɛŋtsɛ he."
title: Ann interviews AI
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "I am a complex computer program but I do not have personal feelings. I am a computer tool, developed by computer programmers to help people with work and fun activities. I do not have any thoughts or feelings. I can do activities for people, like answering questions, writing stories, translating some languages, and summarising information."
ga: "Miji kɔmpiuta nɔ nitsumɔ ko ni mli wa shi mibɛ mi diɛŋtsɛ henumɔi. Miji kɔmpiuta dɛŋdade ko, ni kɔmpiuta he nitsulɔi fee koni eye ebua mɛi yɛ nitsumɔ kɛ hiɛtserɛjiemɔ nifeemɔi amli. Mibɛ susumɔi loo henumɔi komɛi. Mibaanyɛ mafee nibii maha mɛi, tamɔ sanebimɔi ahetoohamɔ, saji aŋmalamɔ, wiemɔi komɛi ashishitsɔɔmɔ, kɛ saji kukufoo."

english: Long time ago, Cassava and Palm lived in a village called Koowa. They were very good friends. They visited each other every day. They were farmers. They worked very hard on their farms.

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: In a certain year, there was no rain. The crops did not grow well. All the plants dried up. People did not have any food to eat. Cassava and Palm decided to travel to another village to look for work.
ga: Afi ko nↄ lԑ, nugbↄ enԑԑԑ yԑ Koowa akrowa lԑ mli. Ŋmↄshi nibii ekwԑԑԑ. Hↄmↄ kple ko ba. Anaaa niyenii aye. Gbi ko be ni duade eyasra tԑŋ lԑ, amԑto amԑyiŋ akԑ amԑbaafa gbԑ koni amԑyatao nitsumↄ kroko amԑtsu.
title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: On their way, they met a woman. "Good afternoon," they greeted her. She responded and asked, "Where are you going?" "We are going to the next village to look for work," said Palm.
ga: Be ni amԑfaa gbԑ lԑ, amԑkԑ yoo ko kpe. "Minaokoo Awo." Duade kԑ tԑŋ ŋa yoo lԑ. Yoo lԑ here amԑ nↄ ekԑԑ, Naejↄ anyԑmimԑi, "Nԑgbԑ nyԑyaa ni etↄ nyԑ nԑkԑ?" "Wↄmiiya wↄyatao nitsumↄ yԑ akrowa kroko nↄ wↄtsu. Bԑ ole akԑ hↄmↄ eba," Tԑŋ kԑԑ.
title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: "What work can you do?" the woman asked. The friends responded, "We can provide food for your family and animals."

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: The woman asked, "What do you need to provide the food?" "Give us land, water and good care," they replied. The woman took them home with her.
ga: Yoo lԑ kԑ amԑtee shia ni ekԑ amԑyahi shi jogbaŋŋ.
title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: One afternoon, Palm tree and Cassava had an argument. Cassava said he was more important than Palm. Palm said he was more important than Cassava.

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: The woman heard them from her room. She came out and asked "Why are you fighting?"
ga: Yoo lԑ nu nↄmↄ lԑ he. Ejekpo yԑ tsu lԑ mli ni ebabi amԑ akԑ, "Mԑni eba ni nyԑnↄↄ?"
title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: "My stems are used for planting. My leaves and peels feed your animals. What does Palm tree do?" asked Cassava.

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: Palm tree laughed, shook his head and said, "Woman, do you remember the palm soup you enjoy so much? I provide it."

english: "I provide the palm oil for preparing kpokpoi and the palm kernel oil for frying fish and meat. How would you prepare stews and gravies without oil?"

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: "Hmmm!" sighed the woman. "Alright friends, I have heard you. I will settle this problem."

english: "Both of you are very important to me. The two of you together make a delicious meal, fufu and palm-nut soup!" said the woman.

title: Cassava and Palm
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Divine Apedo, Elizabeth Nkrumah, Georgina Abbey, illustrations by Brian Wambi

english: The woman prepared palm nut soup with fufu from cassavas. She invited her friends to eat with her. They enjoyed the meal very much. Since then, Cassava and Palm tree have remained good friends.

english: In a city, there lived a beautiful girl whose name was Ella. She was tall, dark skinned, with black hair. She had captivating eyes.
