title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: Ella had a beautiful set of pearl-white teeth. She was a kind and hardworking girl. She never gave her parents problems. The only thing that bothered her parents was her curiosity. She asked very unusual questions.
ga: Ella yɛ ŋmeii fɛfɛji ni tamɔ ŋmeii yɛŋ. Eji gbekɛ yoo ni mli hi ni tsuɔ nii waa. Ekɛ naagbai haaa efɔlɔi kɔkɔɔkɔ. Nɔ pɛ ni gba efɔlɔi anaa ji bɔ ni esumɔɔ ni ele nɔ ni yaa nɔ lɛ. Ebi saji ni yɔɔ naakpɛɛ waa.
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: For example, when her pencil broke, Ella asked her mother, "Mommy, did my pencil go to heaven?" Sometimes her parents did not know how to respond to Ella's many questions so, they kept quiet.
ga: Akɛ nɔkwɛmɔnɔ lɛ, beni e-niŋmaatso lɛ ku lɛ, Ella bi emami akɛ, "Ma, ani mi-niŋmaatso lɛ etee ŋwɛi?" Sanebimɔi babaoo ni Ella biɔ lɛ haa efɔlɔi nijiaŋ jeɔ wui no hewɔ lɛ bei komɛi lɛ, amɛkuɔ amɛhiɛ amɛshwieɔ enɔ.
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: However, Ella's brother, Henry, always listened to Ella's questions. When it was raining she asked, "Is the rain in the cloud crying?" Her brother laughed and answered "No!" He went on to explain that rain falls when vapour in the atmosphere cools.
ga: Shi kɛlɛ, Ella nyɛmi nuu Henry boɔ Ella saji lɛ atoi be fɛɛ be. Beni nugbɔ miinɛ lɛ ebi akɛ, "Ani nugbɔ ni nɛɔ yɛ atatu lɛ mli lɛ miifo?" Enyɛmi nuu lɛ ŋmɔ ni eha hetoo akɛ "Daabi!" Etee nɔ etsɔɔ mli akɛ nugbɔ nɛɔ kɛ́ lasu ni yɔɔ kɔɔyɔɔ lɛ mli jɔ.
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: One day, she decided to go out for a stroll. As she walked, she saw an apple tree and accidentally broke it's branch. "Oh, no! It needs a doctor," Ella said. Surprisingly, the tree answered. "Yes, I need a doctor."
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, ekpɛ eyiŋ akɛ ebaaje kpo eyanyiɛ. Be ni enyiɛ lɛ, ena blɔfo gowa tso ko ni efo enine yɛ oshara mli. "Oh, daabi! Ehe miihia datrɛfonyo," Ella kɛɛ. Nɔ ni yɔɔ naakpɛɛ ji akɛ, tso lɛ ha hetoo. "Hɛɛ, datrɛfonyo he miihia mi."
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: Ella was shocked and asked, "How can you talk?" The tree replied, "I am a tree that can answer all your questions." Ella asked again, "Why can't the boy hear you?" The tree replied, "Because he did not ask."
ga: Ella hie fee lɛ yaa ni ebi akɛ, "Te ooofee tɛŋŋ owie?" Tso lɛ ha hetoo akɛ, "Miji tso ni baanyɛ aha osanebimɔi lɛ fɛɛ ahetoo." Ella bi ekoŋŋ akɛ, "Mɛni hewɔ gbekɛ nuu lɛ nyɛɛɛ anu ohe?" Tso lɛ ha hetoo akɛ, "Ejaakɛ ebiii."
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: Ella ran to her brother and told him what happened. Both of them quickly ran to the tree. Henry asked, "Are you real?" The tree replied, "I am real." They both danced with joy.
ga: Ella jo foi kɛtee enyɛmi nuu lɛ ŋɔɔ ni ekɛɛ lɛ nɔ ni ba lɛ. Amɛyi enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ amɛjo foi oya kɛtee tso lɛ he. Henry bi akɛ, "Ani oyɛ diɛŋtsɛ?" Tso lɛ ha hetoo akɛ, "Miyɛ diɛŋtsɛ." Amɛyi enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ jo kɛ miishɛɛ.
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: Since then, they never disturbed their parents again. Any time they had a question, they went to the apple tree and it answered their questions.
ga: Kɛjɛ nakai beaŋ kɛbaa nɛɛ, amɛgbaaa amɛfɔlɔi anaa dɔŋŋ. Be fɛɛ be ni amɛbaaná sanebimɔ ko lɛ, amɛyaa blɔfo gowa tso lɛ he ni ehaa amɛsanebimɔi lɛ ahetoo.
title: Ella and the Apple Tree of Wisdom
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nneoma Ejeagba, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Nneoma Ejeagba

english: Hospitality
ga: Gbɔfeemɔ
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Madina is the eldest daughter of the Karembe family. The family lives in Bandiagara.
ga: Madina ji Karembe weku lɛ mli biyoo onukpa. Weku lɛ hiɔ Bandiagara.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: One evening, Madina went to close the door. She saw a girl and a boy.
ga: Gbi ko gbɛkɛ lɛ, Madina tee koni eyaŋa shinaa lɛ. Ena gbekɛ yoo kɛ gbekɛ nuu.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Madina was surprised to see two strange children. She called out to her father, "Daddy! Daddy! There are two children at the door."
ga: Madina naa kpɛ ehe beni ena gbekɛbii enyɔ komɛi ni eleee amɛ lɛ. Etsɛ etsɛ, "Da! Da! Gbekɛbii enyɔ yɛ shinaa lɛ naa."
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Father rushed out to the door. When he saw the children, he asked, "Who are you? Where are you from?"
ga: Ataa kɛ oyaiyeli je kpo kɛtee shinaa lɛ naa. Beni ena gbekɛbii lɛ, ebi akɛ, "Namɔ ji nyɛ? Nɛgbɛ nyɛjɛ?"
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: The boy spoke, "I'm Assama, and this is my little sister, Yakôrômo." Assama and Yakôrômo looked tired, scared and sad.
ga: Gbekɛ nuu lɛ wie akɛ, "Atsɛɔ mi Assama, ni minyɛmi yoo fioo, Yakôrômo nɛ." Assama kɛ Yakôrômo tamɔ mɛi ni etɔ amɛ, amɛshe gbeyei ni amɛye awerɛho.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Assama continued to explain, "We've come from the village of Songho, in the rural commune of Doucombo."
ga: Assama tee nɔ etsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Wɔjɛ Songho akrowa lɛ mli, yɛ Doucombo akrowa lɛ mli."
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Father was so shocked that he was speechless. Madina said, "Dad, let them in. They're very tired and hungry. They need us."
ga: Ataa naa kpɛ ehe waa aahu akɛ enyɛɛ ewie. Madina kɛɛ, "Da, ha amɛbote mli. Etɔ amɛ waa ni hɔmɔ miiye amɛ. Wɔhe miihia amɛ."
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Yakôrômo spoke for the first time. "Our village was attacked. We lost our parents. We lost everything."
ga: Yakôrômo wie klɛŋklɛŋ kwraa. "Atutua wɔ akrowa lɛ. Wɔfɔlɔi gboi. Nɔ fɛɛ nɔ eŋmɛɛ wɔ."
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: She continued to speak in a small voice. "We've been walking for days. We don't know where to go or what to do."
ga: Etee nɔ ekɛ gbee bibioo wie. "Wɔ nyiɛ gbii pii. Wɔ le he ni wɔ ya loo nɔ ni wɔ fee."
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Then, with open arms, Father embraced the children. "Come in, children, this is your home. We'll talk about it when you've rested," he said.
ga: Kɛkɛ ni Ataa kɛ eniji ni egbele lɛ fua gbekɛbii lɛ atuu. "Nyɛbotea mli, gbekɛbii, nyɛshia nɛ. Wɔbaawie he kɛji nyɛjɔɔ nyɛhe," ekɛɛ.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: The children joined the family for dinner, the first hot meal they had had in days. Afterward, Madina took Assama and Yakôrômo to their rooms.
ga: Gbekɛbii lɛ bafata weku lɛ he kɛye gbɛkɛ niyenii, ni ji klɛŋklɛŋ niyenii ni mli edɔ ni amɛye yɛ gbii babaoo ni No sɛɛ lɛ, Madina kɛ Assama kɛ Yakôrômo tee amɛtsuji amli.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: From that day, Assama and Yakoromo were considered members of the KAREMBE family. They play and do all the housework with the other children.
ga: Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ nɔ kɛbaa nɛɛ, abuɔ Assama kɛ Yakoromo akɛ KAREMBE weku lɛ mli bii. Amɛkɛ gbekɛbii krokomɛi lɛ shwɛɔ ni amɛtsuɔ shĩa nitsumɔi fɛɛ.
title: Hospitality
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Alassane Sonta, Amadomo dit Issaka Kodio, Djénèba Ganesse, Sira Diakité, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
ga: Hiɛnyiɛlɔi Bibii: Wɔshihilɛhe lɛ he atse
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Lumbazi would have been a good place, but everything was wrong about its environment. There were broken bottles everywhere. Pieces of paper littered the streets and the air smelled very bad.
ga: Kulɛ Lumbazi baafee he ko ni hi, shi nɔ fɛɛ nɔ ejaaa yɛ he ni eyɔɔ lɛ he. Ayɛ tɔi ni ejwara yɛ he fɛɛ he. Woji bibii eyi gbɛjegbɛi lɛ anɔ ni kɔɔyɔɔ lɛ mli je fu waa.
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Children got injured from broken bottles.
ga: Gbekɛbii pila kɛjɛ tɔi ni ejwara lɛ amli.
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: When it was windy, pieces of paper flew and hung on trees and roofs. This kept many people away from visiting Lumbazi.
ga: Kɛ́ kɔɔyɔɔ miitswa lɛ, woji bibii fɔ̃ɔ ni amɛfoɔ tsei kɛ tsũi ayiteŋ. Enɛ ha mɛi babaoo tsi amɛhe kɛjɛ Lumbazi sramɔ he.
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: One day, 9-year-old Chike shared an idea with his friends. "Let us clean our environment together. We can sweep, pick up broken bottles and make waste bins for our houses and streets."
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, Chike ni eye afii 9 lɛ kɛ enanemɛi lɛ gba susumɔ ko he sane. "Nyɛhaa wɔfea ekome kɛtsumɔ wɔshihilɛhe lɛ. Wɔbaanyɛ wɔtsumɔ, wɔjie tɔi ni ejwara ni wɔfee jwɛi ŋtayaai kɛha wɔshiai kɛ gbɛjegbɛi lɛ."
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: "This will help us stay clean. It will attract other communities to visit us," Chike continued.
ga: "Enɛ baaye abua ni wɔhi shi yɛ hetsemɔ mli. Ebaaha akutsei krokomɛi abasara wɔ," Chike tsa nɔ.
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: As he spoke, Obi said, "I will carefully pick up the broken bottles. I will place them where they won't injure us."
ga: Beni ewieɔ lɛ, Obi kɛɛ, "Maŋɔ tɔi ni ejwara lɛ jogbaŋŋ. Makɛwo he ni amɛpilaaa wɔ."
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Felix said, "I will bring one of the old buckets in my house so we can use it as a trash can."
ga: Felix kɛɛ, "Mikɛ googa momo ni yɔɔ mishia lɛ eko baaba koni wɔkɛtsu nii akɛ jwɛi tsinsii."
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: They worked together every day. Since that day, Lumbazi became a healthy and safe place for everyone to stay.
ga: Amɛfeɔ ekome kɛtsuɔ nii daa gbi. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ nɔ kɛbaa nɛɛ, Lumbazi ebatsɔ he ko ni mɔ fɛɛ mɔ baanyɛ ahi ni yɔɔ hewalɛ ni yɔɔ shweshweeshwe.
title: Little Leaders: Keeping our environment clean
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Asuquo, Gideon Eyo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Five foolish men
ga: Hii Buului enumɔ
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Once upon a time, there were five foolish men living together. They shared everything. One day, they ran out of food. They called a meeting. "Where will our next meal come from?" one of them asked.
ga: Be ko ni eho lɛ, hii buului enumɔ hi shi yɛ he kome. Amɛjara nɔ fɛɛ nɔ. Gbi ko lɛ, amɛ niyeníi tã. Amɛtsɛ kpee. "Nɛgbɛ wɔ niyenii ni nyiɛ sɛɛ lɛ baajɛ?" amɛteŋ mɔ kome bi.
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: There was no easy answer to this question because they had no money and no friends in the community. After thinking for a few seconds, one of them said "Let's get going!" The second person asked, "Where?"
ga: Sanebimɔ nɛɛ hetoo ko bɛ ni yɔɔ mlɛo ejaakɛ amɛbɛ shika ni amɛbɛ nanemɛi hu yɛ akutso lɛ mli. Beni amɛsusu he sɛkɛndii fioo komɛi sɛɛ lɛ, amɛteŋ mɔ kome kɛɛ, "Nyɛhaa wɔyaa!" Mɔ ni ji enyɔ lɛ bi akɛ, "Nɛgbɛ?"
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The third person said, "To steal food." The fourth one said, "Won't we get caught?" The fifth person said, "Don't worry about that!" The five men went to the market to steal something to eat.
ga: Mɔ ni ji etɛ lɛ kɛɛ, "Koni wɔju niyenii." Mɔ ni ji ejwɛ lɛ kɛɛ akɛ, "Ani amɔɔɔ wɔ?" Mɔ ni ji enumɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Kaahao ohe yɛ enɛ he!" Hii enumɔ lɛ tee jara lɛ mli koni amɛyaju nɔ ko ni amɛye.
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: As soon as they started stealing, they were caught! The five men were taken to the police station.
ga: Beni amɛbɔi juu pɛ kɛkɛ ni amɔmɔ amɛ! Akɛ hii enumɔ lɛ tee polisifoi anitsumɔhe lɛ.
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: During the investigation, the police asked, "Whose idea was it to steal food?" The men started whispering among themselves. Then they told the police how it happened.
ga: Beni amɛtaoɔ saji amli lɛ, polisifoi lɛ bi akɛ, "Namɔ susumɔ ji akɛ abaju niyenii?" Hii lɛ bɔi amɛhe toiŋwoo. Kɛkɛ ni amɛgba polisifoi lɛ bɔ ni fee ni eba lɛ.
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The first person said, "I only suggested leaving, not stealing." The second person said, "I was curious about where we were going." The third person said, "We all agreed to look for food."
ga: Mɔ klɛŋklɛŋ lɛ kɛɛ, "Mikɛ ŋaawoo ha akɛ wɔshi kɛkɛ, shi jeee juu." Mɔ ni ji enyɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Miitao male he ni wɔyaa." Mɔ ni ji etɛ lɛ kɛɛ, "Wɔ fɛɛ wɔkpɛlɛ nɔ akɛ wɔbaatao niyenii."
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The fourth person said, "I warned all of us that we're going to be caught." And the fifth person said, "We all know we are thieves, and that's why I said, 'Don't worry about it'."
ga: Mɔ ni ji ejwɛ lɛ kɛɛ, "Mibɔ wɔ fɛɛ kɔkɔ akɛ abaamɔ wɔ." Ni mɔ ni ji enumɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Wɔ fɛɛ wɔle akɛ julɔi ji wɔ, ni no hewɔ ni mikɛɛ, 'Kaahao ohe' lɛ."
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: After hearing this, the police understood that all five men were involved in theft. The police officer concluded, "It is a good idea to share everything, except bad ideas!"
ga: Beni polisifoi lɛ nu enɛ sɛɛ lɛ, amɛnu shishi akɛ hii enumɔ lɛ fɛɛ kɛ amɛhe wo juu mli. Polisifonyo lɛ mu sane naa akɛ, "Eji jwɛŋmɔ kpakpa akɛ oooja nɔ fɛɛ nɔ, ja susumɔi gbohii!"
title: Five foolish men
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Chuol Dow Wich, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Maṱodzi's kindness
ga: Maṱodzi mlihilɛ lɛ
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: There once was a girl named Maṱodzi. Maṱodzi lived in a village with her mother and grandmother.
ga: Be ko ni eho lɛ, gbekɛ yoo ko yɛ ni atsɛɔ lɛ Maṱodzi. Maṱodzi kɛ emami kɛ enaa hi akrowa ko mli.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: One day, Maṱodzi’s mother asked her to take a message to her aunt in another village. “Follow the route we usually use,” her mother reminded Maṱodzi.
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, Maṱodzi nyɛ kɛɛ lɛ akɛ ekɛ sane ko ayahã emami nyɛmi yoo ni yɔɔ akrowa kroko lɛ. Emami kai Maṱodzi akɛ, "Nyɛnyiɛa gbɛ ni wɔfɔɔ nɔ kɛyaa lɛ nɔ."
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Maṱodzi followed the familiar path to her aunt’s house and delivered the message. As she was on her way home, she heard a weak voice nearby saying, “Please help me.”
ga: Maṱodzi nyiɛ gbɛ ni ale lɛ nɔ kɛtee emami nyɛmi yoo lɛ shĩa ni ekɛ sane lɛ tee. Beni enyiɛ gbɛ kɛmiiya shia lɛ, enu gbee ko ni bɛ hewalɛ ni bɛŋkɛ lɛ ni miikɛɛ akɛ, "Ofainɛ ye obua mi."
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Maṱodzi looked around and saw a woman lying on the road. She greeted the woman and asked, “Why are you lying here?”
ga: Maṱodzi kwɛ ehe kɛkpe ni ena yoo ko ka gbɛ lɛ nɔ. Eŋa yoo lɛ ni ebi lɛ akɛ, "Mɛni hewɔ okã shi yɛ biɛ lɛ?"
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: The woman replied, “I am weak and ill, and very far from my home.” Maṱodzi felt pity for the woman.
ga: Yoo lɛ ha hetoo akɛ, "Mibɛ hewalɛ ni hela mɔ mi, ni mikɛ mishia lɛ teŋ jɛkɛ waa." Yoo lɛ he fee Maṱodzi mɔbɔ.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: She said to the woman, “I will take you to my home because it’s near.” Maṱodzi helped the woman to get up. They walked very slowly until they arrived.
ga: Ekɛɛ yoo lɛ akɛ, "Makɛ bo aya mishia ejaakɛ ebɛŋkɛ." Maṱodzi ye ebua yoo lɛ ni ete shi. Amɛnyiɛ blɛoo waa kɛyashi amɛyashɛ jɛmɛ.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Maṱodzi and her mother and grandmother took care of the woman until she was well.
ga: Maṱodzi kɛ emami kɛ enaa kwɛ yoo lɛ nɔ aahu kɛyashi ehe wa lɛ.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: The woman was very grateful to them for looking after her. She praised Maṱodzi for being courageous and caring.
ga: Yoo lɛ hiɛ sɔ amɛ waa akɛ amɛkwɛ lɛ. Ejie Maṱodzi yi akɛ eyɛ ekãa ni esusuɔ mɔ he.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: The woman said to Maṱodzi and her family, “I will never forget what you did for me. After three days have passed, I want you to make two wishes.”
ga: Yoo lɛ kɛɛ Maṱodzi kɛ eweku lɛ akɛ, "Mihiɛ kpaŋ nɔ ni nyɛfee nyɛhã mi lɛ nɔ kɔkɔɔkɔ. Kɛ́ gbii etɛ ho lɛ, miisumɔ ni ofee nibii enyɔ ni osumɔɔ."
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: After three days, Maṱodzi and her mother and grandmother made two wishes. Their first wish was to have a beautiful house.
ga: Gbii etɛ sɛɛ lɛ, Maṱodzi kɛ emami kɛ enaa fee nibii enyɔ ni amɛsumɔɔ. Nɔ klɛŋklɛŋ ni amɛshwe ji ni amɛná shĩa fɛfɛo ko.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: The second wish was to have a forest next to the house so that they didn’t have to walk far to fetch wood. Both their wishes came true, just as the woman had said.
ga: Nɔ ni ji enyɔ ni amɛsumɔɔ ji ni amɛná koo ko yɛ shia lɛ masɛi koni amɛkanyiɛ shɔŋŋ kɛyahe tsei. Amɛyi enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ ashwelɛi lɛ ba mli, taakɛ yoo lɛ kɛɛ lɛ pɛpɛɛpɛ.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Maṱodzi and her family lived happily in their lovely house by the forest.
ga: Maṱodzi kɛ eweku lɛ hi amɛshia fɛfɛo ni yɔɔ koo lɛ masɛi lɛ mli kɛ miishɛɛ.
title: Maṱodzi's kindness
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Tshedza Tlhako, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: King Kayanja and his daughter
ga: Maŋtsɛ Okaija Kɛ Ebiyoo Lɛ
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Long, long ago there was a king called Kayanja. He lived in a palace with his queen and their daughter, Princess Apenyo. Princess Apenyo was such a beautiful young woman that every man wanted to marry her. But king Kayanja demanded a very high bride price for the princess.
ga: Be ko ni eho jeeŋmɔ lɛ, maŋtsɛ ko hi shi ni atsɛɔ lɛ maŋtsɛ Okaija. Ekɛ maŋnyɛ lɛ kɛ ebiyoo Oboshi hi shi yɛ maŋtsɛ we lɛ. Oboshi hefɛo sɔɔŋ hewɔ lɛ, hii fɛɛ sumɔɔ akɛ amɛkɛ lɛ ahi shi. Shi yinii ni maŋtsɛ Okaija heɔ lɛ jara wa tsɔ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Near king Kayanja's palace lived a chief called Aludah the Great. He was called "the Great" because everybody in the neighbourhood obeyed him, and he was very violent to anyone who disobeyed him! Chief Aludah's wife had recently died of malaria, and he wanted another wife.
ga: Maŋtsɛ ko hi shi yɛ maŋtsɛ Okaija we lɛ masɛi ni atsɛɔ lɛ Nii Obodai Kpeteŋkple. Atsɛɔ lɛ "Kpeteŋkple" ejaakɛ mɔ fɛɛ mɔ yeɔ ewiemɔ nɔ yɛ akutso lɛ mli. (Enyafiɔ mɛi ni yeee ewiemɔ nɔ!) Nyɛsɛɛ nɛɛ, atridii gbe maŋtsɛ Obodai ŋa hewɔ lɛ eetao ŋa kroko.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: So the fat old chief went to king Kayanja to offer bride wealth for the young princess. While the two men were discussing the price, the maid Kakembo overheard their conversation. Maid Kakembo was very close to princess Apenyo.
ga: Enɛ hewɔ lɛ, maŋtsɛ nuumo tɔbɔɔ lɛ tee maŋtsɛ Okaija ŋɔ koni eyaha maŋtsɛ biyoo fioo lɛ yinii. Be ni hii enyɔ lɛ yeɔ yinii lɛ naa lɛ, abaawa Lajɛ nu sane lɛ. Enaanyo jogbaŋŋ ji maŋtsɛ biyoo Oboshi.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Chief Aludah agreed to give half of his wealth to king Kayanja, including a needle, which was also part of the bride price. Preparations were made in secret for the wedding between chief Aludah and princess Apenyo. The king knew that his daughter would not be happy with this decision.
ga: Maŋtsɛ Obodai kplɛ nɔ akɛ ekɛ enɔbaa lɛ mlijaa fa, kɛ abui ko ni fata yinii lɛ he lɛ baaha maŋtsɛ Okaija. Ato gbɛjianɔ kɛha maŋtsɛ Obodai kɛ maŋtsɛ biyoo Oboshi gbalamlibotemɔ nigii. Maŋtsɛ lɛ le faŋŋ akɛ ebiyoo lɛ banaŋ nifeemɔ nɛɛ he miishɛɛ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: One week before the royal wedding day, maid Kakembo approached Apenyo. "My dear Princess, your father has organised your wedding with chief Aludah, and it will take place in one week."
ga: Be ni eshɛ otsi kome kɛha ablade yoo kpeemɔ nɛɛ, abaawa Lajɛ tee Oboshi ŋɔ. "Minaanyo kpakpa maŋtsɛ biyoo, otsɛ ataa eto gbɛjianɔ kɛha okɛ maŋtsɛ Obodai ayɛmfrofeemɔ otsi nibaa nɛɛ," Lajɛ kɛɛ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Princess Apenyo was shocked and at first didn't know what to do. Then she thought, "I will never marry chief Aludah, that fat old man. Never! I must hurry to Trevor and see what he can do before it's too late." Trevor was princess Apenyo's boyfriend.
ga: Sane lɛ fee maŋtsɛ biyoo Oboshi naakpɛɛ ni enaaa bɔ ni efeɔ ehe ehaa. Kɛkɛ ni ejwɛŋ, "Mikɛ maŋtsɛ Obodai ehiii shi kɔkɔɔkɔ, nakai nuumo tɔbɔɔ lɛ. Sua! Mafee oya kɛyana Taki ni makwɛ nɔ ni ebaafee nɔŋŋ." Taki lɛ, maŋtsɛ biyoo Oboshi shwɛbilɔ nuu ni.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: That night Apenyo crept out of the palace. If her father discovered where she was going he would be very angry. She ran through the thick, dark forest over rocks and shrubs. When finally she arrived at Trevor's house she was tired and thirsty.
ga: Nakai gbɛkɛ lɛ, Oboshi shi maŋtsɛ we lɛ nigii. Etsɛ ataa mli baafu kɛji eyɔse he ni eyaa. Ewo foi kɛtsɔ koo gbidii kabitii lɛ mli. Etsɔmɔ tɛsai kɛ tsei amli kɛyashi naagbee lɛ eyashɛ Taki ŋɔ. Be ni eshɛ Taki shia lɛ etɔ lɛ, hɔmɔ miiye lɛ ni kuma hu miiye lɛ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: "My love, why have you run all this long distance alone and at such a time of night?" asked Trevor. He fetched water for her and allowed her to rest. Trevor could not settle down while he waited for Apenyo to talk.
ga: "Misuɔlɔ, mɛɛba okome ojofoi gbɛ kakadaŋŋ nɛɛ kɛtsɔ duŋ nɛɛ mli be nɛɛ mli?" Taki bi. Eyɛ nu eha lɛ ni ehani ejɔɔ ehe. Taki fee hahaaha be ni emɛɔ Oboshi ni ebɔ lɛ amaniɛ lɛ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: "My dear princess, what is the problem?" asked Trevor. Apenyo breathed heavily and said sadly, "My father wants to marry me off to chief Aludah the Great. But I can't marry that horrible man. Trevor, I want to marry you even if you are poor. I am ready to suffer. I love you."
ga: "Minaanyo kpakpa maŋtsɛ biyoo, mɛni sane eba?" Taki bi. Oboshi mu waa ni ekɛ awerɛho wie, "Mitsɛ ataa miitao ni ekɛ mi aha Obodai wulu gbala. Shi minyɛɛɛ mikɛ nakai nuu gbeyeigbeyei lɛ ahi shi. Taki, bo nɔŋŋ mikɛ baahi shi kɛji ohiafo tete ji bo. Mifee klalo akɛ mananɔ. Misumɔ bo."
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: "But princess, I have nothing to pay as your bride price, you know I'm a poor boy," cried Trevor. Apenyo replied, "I know, but it's only you I can get married to." She thought for a while and said, "Let's go to Kategga the boatman and ask him to take us across the river. That way we can escape and my father will never find us."
ga: "Shi maŋtsɛ biyoo, mibɛ nɔ ko nɔ ko ni mikɛbaayafee ohe nii," Taki wie kɛ yaafo. Oboshi here nɔ, "Mile, shi bo pɛ mikɛ baahi shi." Ejwɛŋ be saŋŋ ni ekɛɛ, "Ha wɔya Kwao, lɛlɛkudɔlɔ lɛ ŋɔ koni ekɛwɔ afo faa lɛ kɛya faa lɛ sɛɛ. Wɔbaashi biɛ kwraa ni mitsɛ ataa enaŋ wɔ dɔŋŋ."
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Back at the palace, king Kayanja had discovered princess Apenyo's disappearance. He ordered his subjects to search for her everywhere. The king's guards, soldiers, and everyone else searched, but they couldn't find the princess. They went back to the king and told him that Apenyo was nowhere to be seen. "Then go back and search again," King Kayanja ordered. He was very annoyed.
ga: Yɛ maŋtsɛ we lɛ, maŋtsɛ Okaija yɔse akɛ ebi yoo Oboshi ejo foi hewɔ lɛ, etsu etsulɔi lɛ ni amɛyatao lɛ yɛ akrowa lɛ mli he fɛɛ he. Maŋtsɛ hebulɔi lɛ, asrafoi kɛ maŋbii lɛ fɛɛ yatao Oboshi shi amɛnaaa lɛ. Amɛku amɛsɛɛ kɛtee maŋtsɛ lɛ ŋɔ ni amɛ hani ele akɛ amɛnaaa Oboshi yɛ he ko he ko. "Kɛ nakai lɛ, nyɛ yaa jwɛiaŋ nyɛyataoa lɛ," maŋtsɛ Okaija fa. Emli efu diɛŋtsɛ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: As Princess Apenyo and Trevor hurried to the riverbank, dark clouds began gathering in the sky. A heavy storm was coming.
ga: Be ni Oboshi kɛ Taki yaa faa lɛ naa lɛ, atatu tuŋ komɛi bɔi amɛhe naabuamɔ yɛ ŋwɛi. Ahum wulu ko miiba.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Kategga the boatman was mooring his boat when the young couple approached him. Trevor asked Kategga to row them across the river. Kategga refused to accept, explaining that a heavy storm was fast approaching, and it would be too dangerous.
ga: Taki kɛ Oboshi yanina Kwao, lɛlɛkudɔlɔ lɛ ni eeŋmɛ sɛkɛ bɔ ni afee ni lɛlɛ lɛ adamɔ shi. Taki kɛɛ Kwao ni ekɛ amɛ afo faa lɛ. Kwao ekpɛlɛɛɛ. Ehani amɛle akɛ ahum wulu ko miiba kɛ foi hewɔ lɛ, gbɛfaa nakai beiaŋ baafee ablaŋ.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Trevor insisted and explained to Kategga why they must cross. He then put his hand deep in his pocket and took out a cowrie shell to give to Kategga. When Kategga heard their story and saw the beautiful shell, he felt sorry for them. He agreed to row them across the river in spite of the weather.
ga: Taki bi Kwao ekoŋŋ ni ekɛɛ lɛ nɔ hewɔ ni etaoɔ ni amɛfo faa lɛ. Ekɛ enine wo ekotoku lɛ mli ni ejie terema kɛha Kwao. Be ni Kwao nu sane lɛ ni ena terema fɛfɛo lɛ, amɛhenii fee lɛ mɔbɔ. No hewɔ lɛ ekpɛlɛ akɛ ekɛ amɛbaafo faa lɛ bɔ fɛɛ bɔ ni je lɛ mli etsake eha.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: When King Kayanja and chief Aludah reached the bank, they saw the three people in the boat. They realised that the young lovers had escaped. Heavy winds rocked the boat and Kategga could no longer control it. King Kayanja shouted, "Apenyo, please come back! I forgive you. I will never punish you or Trevor."
ga: Ahum wulu ko tswa bɔ ni Kwao nyɛɛɛ ewiri lɛlɛ lɛ dɔŋŋ. Maŋtsɛ Okaija bo waa, "Oboshi, ofainɛ kuu osɛɛ oba! Mikɛ o eshai eke bo, ni migbalaaa nyɛ toi." Kwao gbala lɛlɛ lɛ kɛba faa lɛ toi ni eha amɛbote mli. Ekɔ tablɔ lɛ ni ebɔi lɛlɛ lɛ wirimɔ. Be ni maŋtsɛ Okaija kɛ Obodai shɛ faa lɛ toi lɛ, ena mɛi etɛ lɛ tara lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Amɛyɔse akɛ suɔlɔi lɛ ejo foi.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: But, it was too late. The boat tipped over and the three people were thrown into the wild water. They all drowned. After that day, everyone in king Kayanja's kingdom could marry anyone they wanted, rich or poor.
ga: Shi ewiemɔ nɛɛ kpesɛɛ kwraa tsɔ. Lɛlɛ lɛ butu ni mɛi etɛ lɛ nyɔ yɛ nu himahima lɛ mli. Amɛ fɛɛ amɛ nyɔmɔ yɛ nu lɛ shishi. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ, gbɛ gbele kɛha mɔ fɛɛ mɔ ni yɔɔ maŋtsɛ Okaija we lɛ mli akɛ, amɛkɛ mɔ ni amɛsumɔ abote gbalashihilɛ mli; shikatsɛ jio, ohiafo jio.
title: King Kayanja and his daughter
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Amana Yunus, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Natalie Propa

english: Magezi's drum
ga: Magezi obonu lɛ
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Magezi starts drumming his black and white drum.
ga: Magezi jeɔ e-bonu diŋ kɛ eyɛŋ lɛ tswaa shishi.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Children gather around him. They sing along with the drum.
ga: Gbekɛbii buaa amɛhe naa kɛbɔleɔ lɛ. Amɛláa kɛfataa obonu lɛ he.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: They sing, “Who is Masingita married to? She is married to one of our fellows.”
ga: Amɛlaa akɛ, "Namɔ Masingita kɛbote gbalashihilɛ mli? Ekɛ wɔnanemɛi lɛ ateŋ."
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Women dance around at the sound of the drum.
ga: Yei joɔ kɛbɔleɔ amɛhe kɛ amɛnuɔ obonu lɛ gbɛɛmɔ.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Men roll on the ground with up and down movements.
ga: Hii kokoloɔ shikpɔŋ kɛ ŋwɛi kɛ shikpɔŋ nɔ nyiɛmɔi.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Mudungwazi rolls his eyes and does his funny dance.
ga: Mudungwazi tsɔ ehiŋmɛii amli ni efee ejo ni yɔɔ ŋmɔlɔ lɛ.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Old men whistle and shake their heads to the drumbeat.
ga: Hiimei kpaa bɛlɛ ni amɛwosoɔ amɛyitsei kɛyaa gbee ni akɛtswaa lɛ nɔ.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Old women sway their hips and ululate. Everyone enjoys Magezi’s drumming.
ga: Yemei lɛ sha amɛhɛmli kɛ miishɛɛ lalai. Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ sumɔɔ Magezi obunu yii lɛ.
title: Magezi's drum
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Hlekane Paulinah Baloyi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Language - Ga

english: Mama Sophie, the brave one
ga: Mama Sophie, mɔ ni yɔɔ ekãa lɛ
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: On one hot summer day, Khosi was pacing to and fro, wondering what to do. Her mother had gone to the fields leaving Khosi behind. “What shall I do with myself?” said Khosi to herself.
ga: Yɛ hulutsoo be mli gbi ko ni edɔ waa lɛ, Khosi miiho kɛmiiya kɛmiiba, ni eesusu nɔ ni ebaafee lɛ he. No mli lɛ, emami etee ŋmɔ mli ni eshi Khosi. "Mɛni mafee mi diɛŋtsɛ mihe?" Khosi kɛɛ ehe.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: An idea flashed into Khosi’s mind. “I am going to swim at the river, but who will go with me?” thought Khosi. At that moment Mama Sophie passed by on her way to the river. She was carrying a big basket full of clothes.
ga: Jwɛŋmɔ ko ba Khosi jwɛŋmɔ mli. "Miiya nu yɛ faa lɛ naa, shi namɔ baafata mihe?" Khosi susu he. Nakai beaŋ lɛ, Mama Sophie ho kɛmiiya faa lɛ naa. Ehiɛ kɛntɛŋ agbo ko ni atadei eyi mli obɔ.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: “I am going to follow Mama Sophie to the river!” said Khosi to herself. “May I please go with you to the river?” asked Khosi. Mama Sophie smiled and nodded. Along the way, Nozipho joined them. Nozipho never liked swimming but enjoyed watching others swim.
ga: "Miiya ni mayanyiɛ Mama Sophie sɛɛ kɛya faa lɛ naa!" Khosi kɛɛ ehe. "Ofainɛ, ani manyɛ mikɛ bo aya faa lɛ naa?" Khosi bi lɛ. Mama Sophie ŋmɔ ni ekɛ ehiɛ tsɔɔ ŋwɛi. Yɛ gbɛ lɛ nɔ lɛ, Nozipho bafata amɛhe. Nozipho sumɔɔɔ nu wumɔ kɔkɔɔkɔ shi esumɔɔ ni ekwɛ mɛi krokomɛi ni wuɔ nu lɛ.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: At the river Khosi said to herself, “Today, I am finished with swimming in shallow waters, like a baby! I am going to show everyone that I can swim in deep waters too.” She plunged into the river. Splash! Nozipho watched from a safe distance.
ga: Yɛ faa lɛ naa lɛ, Khosi kɛɛ ehe akɛ, "Ŋmɛnɛ, migbe nu ni mli kwɔɔɔ mli wumɔ naa, tamɔ abifao! Miiya ni matsɔɔ mɔ fɛɛ mɔ akɛ mi hu manyɛ mawu yɛ nu ni mli kwɔ mli." Ekɛ ehe wo faa lɛ mli. Shwiemɔ! Nozipho kwɛ kɛjɛ he ko ni yɔɔ shweshweeshwe.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: As Nozipho watched, all the children were having fun in the river. They were swimming noisily. They shouted at each other happily in the water.
ga: Beni Nozipho kwɛɔ lɛ, no mli lɛ gbekɛbii lɛ fɛɛ miijie amɛhiɛtserɛ yɛ faa lɛ mli. Amɛmiiwu nu lɛ kɛ hoofeemɔ. Amɛbolɔ amɛwo amɛhe kɛ miishɛɛ yɛ nu lɛ mli.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Nozipho looked again carefully, something looked different. Khosi was swimming far away from the other children. Nozipho went closer and looked again. Terrified by what she saw, she ran towards the women doing their washing by the river. “Help! Khosi is drowning,” screamed Nozipho.
ga: Nozipho kwɛ jogbaŋŋ ekoŋŋ, nɔ ko tamɔ nɔ ni yɔɔ srɔto. Khosi miiwu nu yɛ he ko ni kɛ gbekɛbii krokomɛi lɛ teŋ jɛkɛ. Nozipho tsi ebɛŋkɛ ni ekwɛ ekoŋŋ. Akɛni nɔ ni ena lɛ wo lɛ gbeyei hewɔ lɛ, ejo foi kɛtee yei ni miifɔ amɛnibii ahe nii yɛ faa lɛ naa lɛ aŋɔɔ. Nozipho bolɔ akɛ, "Aye abua me! Nuŋmi Khosi.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: In a split second, Mama Sophie jumped into the water. Down the river she swam. She dived under the water, then up, then under again, looking for Khosi. She grabbed Khosi by the arm and swam to shallow water. Then, Mama Sophia carried Khosi out of the river.
ga: Yɛ ŋmlɛ mlijaa kome mli lɛ, Mama Sophie tu kɛbote nu lɛ mli. Efo faa lɛ shishi. Ekɛ ehe wo nu lɛ shishi, kɛkɛ ni ekwɔ, kɛkɛ ni ekɛ ehe wo shishi ekoŋŋ, ni etao Khosi. Emɔ Khosi nine mli ni efo kɛtee nu ni mli kwɔɔɔ mli lɛ mli. Kɛkɛ ni, Mama Sophia wo Khosi kɛjɛ faa lɛ mli.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Mama Sophie hurried past the group of children and women who were wailing and shouting. Nozipho ran behind her as she hurried to the village clinic, holding Khosi on her back.
ga: Mama Sophie kɛ oyaiyeli tsɔ gbekɛbii kɛ yei akuu ni miifó ni amɛmiibolɔ lɛ hiɛ. Nozipho jo foi kɛnyiɛ esɛɛ beni ekɛ oyaiyeli tee akrowa lɛ helatsamɔhe lɛ, ni ehiɛ Khosi yɛ esɛɛ lɛ.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: At the clinic Mama was met by nurse Noxolo who ran to help. Nurse Noxolo quickly took Khosi into a room and other nurses hurried to assist. “She is ok! We are lucky that she was not under water for a second longer!” said Nurse Noxolo.
ga: Yɛ helatsamɔhe lɛ, nɛsifonyo Noxolo ni jo foi kɛtee koni eyaye ebua lɛ kɛ Mama kpe. Nɛsifonyo Noxolo kɛ Khosi tee tsu ko mli oya ni nɛsifonyo krokomɛi fee oya koni amɛbaye amɛbua. "Eyɛ jogbaŋŋ! Wɔyɛ naagba akɛ ebɛ nu shishi ŋmlɛ kome po dɔŋŋ!" nɛsifonyo Noxolo kɛɛ.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Mama Sophie sighed a huge sigh of relief. Everyone at the clinic congratulated her for her bravery and skill with swimming. “I am grateful I could save a life,” said Mama Sophie humbly.
ga: Mama Sophie mu hejɔɔmɔ kple ko. waa. Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ ni yɔɔ helatsamɔhe lɛ jie lɛ yi yɛ ekãa kɛ ŋaa ni eyɔɔ yɛ nu mli shwiili mli lɛ hewɔ. Mama Sophie kɛ heshibaa kɛɛ akɛ, "Miida shi akɛ minyɛ mihere mɔ ko wala yiwala."
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: News reached the local chief. She sent a messenger to call Mama Sophie. Mama Sophie explained to the chief how she became a good swimmer. “As a child, my friend lived across the river. Water was part of our everyday lives. We had to learn to swim!” she said.
ga: Adafitswaa lɛ yashɛ maŋtsɛ lɛ ŋɔɔ. Etsu bɔfo ko koni eyatsɛ Mama Sophie. Mama Sophie tsɔɔ onukpa lɛ bɔ ni fee ni ebatsɔ nu mli shwiili kpakpa lɛ mli. "Beni gbekɛ ji mi lɛ, minaanyo lɛ hiɔ faa lɛ naa. Nu fata wɔ daa gbi shihilɛ he. Ehe bahia ni wɔkase nu wumɔ!" ekɛɛ.
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: The chief called a meeting and announced that she would give a reward to Mama Sophie for her brave deed. Women ululated, men whistled, the children shouted in excitement. From that day, children liked to follow Mama Sophie, singing, “Nothing can touch me, with Mama Sophie, the courageous one, by my side!”
ga: Maŋtsɛ lɛ tsɛ kpee ni etswa adafi akɛ ebaaha Mama Sophie nyɔmɔ yɛ ekãa ni efee lɛ hewɔ. Yei bolɔ, hii kpa bɛlɛ, gbekɛbii lɛ bolɔ kɛ miishɛɛ. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ nɔ kɛbaa nɛɛ, gbekɛbii sumɔɔ ni amɛnyiɛ Mama Sophie sɛɛ, ni amɛlá akɛ, "Nɔ ko nɔ ko nyɛŋ ata mihe, kɛ Mama Sophie, mɔ ni yɔɔ ekãa lɛ, yɛ mimasɛi!"
title: Mama Sophie, the brave one
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Thandiwe Dlodlo, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Cat and Dog are friends
ga: Nanemɛi ji Alonte kɛ Gbee
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Cat and Dog are good friends. They decided to visit their friend, Chick on his birthday. Chick lived in another village. It would take Cat and Dog two days to arrive.
ga: Nanemɛi kpakpai ji Alonte kɛ Gbee. Amɛkpɛ amɛyiŋ akɛ amɛbaayasara amɛnaanyo, wuɔbi yɛ efɔmɔ gbi nɔ. Wuɔbi yɛ akrowa kroko mli. Ebaahe Alonte kɛ Gbee gbii enyɔ dani amɛbashɛ jɛmɛ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Cat and Dog behaved in very different ways. Dog loved to eat and sleep and was mischievous at times. Cat was kind, generous and could be relied on. They met at Dog’s place to plan their journey.
ga: Alonte kɛ Gbee jie amɛjeŋ yɛ gbɛ̀i srɔtoi kwraa nɔ. Gbee sumɔɔ niyeli kɛ wɔɔ ni efeɔ basabasa yɛ bei komɛi amli. Alonte mli hi, ehaa nii babaoo ni abaanyɛ akɛ he afɔ̃ enɔ. Amɛkpe yɛ Gbee shia koni amɛto amɛ gbɛfaa lɛ he gbɛjianɔ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: “I will bring food for the first day,” Dog offered. “I will bring for the second day,” said Cat. They wrote everything down so they would not forget.
ga: Gbee kɛ ehe ha akɛ, "Mikɛ niyenii kɛha klɛŋklɛŋ gbi lɛ baaba." Alonte kɛɛ akɛ, "Mikɛ gbi ni ji enyɔ lɛ baaba." Amɛŋmala nɔ fɛɛ nɔ amɛshwie shi koni amɛhiɛ akakpa nɔ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: “It will be exciting to see Chick soon. It’s been a while since we saw our friend,” Dog said as he walked Cat home. “Thank you for walking me home,” Cat said to Dog.
ga: "Ebaafee miishɛɛ akɛ wɔbaana Wuɔbi etsɛŋ. Be ko eho kɛjɛ be mli ni wɔna wɔnaanyo lɛ," Gbee kɛɛ beni ekɛ Alonte nyiɛɔ kɛyaa shia lɛ. Alonte kɛɛ Gbee akɛ, "Oyiwaladɔŋŋ akɛ okɛ mi tee shia."
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: They met up very early the following day to start their journey. They sang and danced happily on the way. After a while, they rested under a big tree. “I am hungry! Let’s eat,” said Cat.
ga: Amɛkpe mra waa enɔ jetsɛremɔ lɛ koni amɛje amɛ gbɛfaa lɛ shishi. Amɛlá ni amɛjo kɛ miishɛɛ yɛ gbɛ lɛ nɔ. Be fioo sɛɛ lɛ, amɛjɔɔ amɛhe yɛ tso agbo ko shishi. "Hɔmɔ miiye mi! Ha wɔ ye nii," Alonte kɛɛ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Dog hurriedly dished food into two bowls. The food was oily and watery. Cat asked, “Is this the food you brought for both of us?” Cat was angry because her friend did not bring the food they agreed on. She did not eat Dog’s food.
ga: Gbee kɛ oyaiyeli shwie niyenii ewo tsɛnsii enyɔ mli. Niyenii lɛ mli eyi kɛ fɔ kɛ nu. Alonte bi akɛ, "Ani niyenii ni okɛbaha wɔyi enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ nɛ?" Alonte mli fu ejaakɛ enaanyo lɛ kɛ niyenii ni amɛkpɛlɛ nɔ lɛ baaa. Eyeee Gbee niyenii.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: “Why are you waiting?” Dog asked. He hoped that Cat would stop complaining and eat. Annoyed, Cat asked, “Why did you bring food that only you like?” Dog was eating so fast that the bowl slipped. All Dog’s food spilled on the ground.
ga: "Mɛni hewɔ omɛɛɔ?" Gbee bi. Ehiɛ ka nɔ akɛ Alonte baakpa huhuuhu wiemɔ ni eye nii. Akɛni Alonte mli efu hewɔ lɛ, ebi akɛ, "Mɛni hewɔ okɛ niyenii ni bo pɛ osumɔɔ ba lɛ?" Gbee miiye nii oya aahu akɛ tsɛnsi lɛ jɛ edeŋ. Gbee niyenii lɛ fɛɛ shwie shikpɔŋ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: “Don’t worry my friend,” Cat said. Cat took out the most beautiful sandwiches. She began to eat. Dog looked at Cat’s food with pleading eyes. When Cat finished eating, she packed up and told Dog, “Can we continue our journey?”
ga: Alonte kɛɛ akɛ, "Kaahao ohe minaanyo." Alonte jie sandwitsii ni yɔɔ fɛo fe fɛɛ lɛ. Ebɔi niyeli. Gbee kwɛ Alonte niyenii lɛ kɛ hiŋmɛii ni kpaɔ fai. Beni Alonte ye nii egbe naa lɛ, ekɛ enibii lɛ to ni ekɛɛ Gbee akɛ, "Ani wɔbaanyɛ wɔtsa wɔ gbɛfaa lɛ nɔ?"
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: They did not talk for the rest of the journey. Dog’s stomach rumbled from hunger. That evening, Cat dished up for herself. She went to sleep happy that she had brought enough food. Dog went to sleep hungry.
ga: Amɛwieee yɛ gbɛfaa lɛ mli be ni eshwɛ lɛ fɛɛ mli. Gbee musu lɛ tswa kɛjɛ hɔmɔ mli. Nakai gbɛkɛ lɛ, Alonte shwie niyenii eha ehe. Ewɔ kɛ miishɛɛ akɛ ekɛ niyenii ni fa bɔ ni sa eba. Gbee tee wɔɔ kɛ hɔmɔ.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: In the morning, Cat served herself a small breakfast. Dog couldn’t stop looking at Cat’s food. Cat offered Dog some food. Dog said, “Forgive me. I was very selfish.” Cat answered, “Let’s eat together.” They sat down to eat.
ga: Leebi lɛ, Alonte ha ehe leebi niyenii bibioo ko. Gbee nyɛɛɛ akpa Alonte niyenii lɛ kwɛmɔ. Alonte ha Gbee niyenii ko. Gbee kɛɛ, "Kɛ ke mi. Misusu mi pɛ he." Alonte ha hetoo akɛ, "Ha ni wɔ ye nii." Amɛtara shi koni amɛye nii.
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: As they continued with their journey, they were friends again! They arrived at Chick’s house in time. “How was your journey my friends?” Chick asked. Smiling at each other, Cat and Dog answered, “Very good.”
ga: Beni amɛyaa nɔ amɛfãa gbɛ lɛ, amɛbatsɔmɔ nanemɛi ekoŋŋ! Amɛyashɛ Wuɔbi shia yɛ bei ni sa mli. "Te nyɛ gbɛfaa lɛ tee nɔ eha tɛŋŋ minanemɛi?" Wuɔbi lɛ bi. Beni amɛmiiŋmɔ amɛhe lɛ, Alonte kɛ Gbee ha hetoo akɛ, "Ehi waa."
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: It was indeed a great birthday party. They ate, sang and danced!
ga: Eji fɔmɔ gbijurɔyeli kpeteŋkpele diɛŋtsɛ. Amɛye nii, amɛla ni amɛjo!
title: Cat and Dog are friends
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Yamkela Mbhele, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Busisiwe Ndlovu

english: Why Ajao was not buried
ga: Nɔ Hewɔ ni Anaaa Afũ Ajao
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: Ajao, a bat, lay in his house very ill. There was no one to attend to him.
ga: Ajao, aputupata ko, he baye be ko. Ekã hela saa mli yɛ eshia lɛ. Mɔ ko bɛ ni kwɛ enɔ.
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: Then, Ajao died.
ga: Ajao bagbo.
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The neighbours said, "Ajao is dead. We must call his relations to come and bury him."
ga: Ajao henɔi lɛ kɛɛ, "Ajao egbo. Esa ni wɔyatsɛ ewebii lɛ ni amɛba koni amɛbafũ lɛ."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The neighbours went and called the birds saying, "A relative of yours is dead."
ga: Henɔi lɛ tee amɛyatsɛ loofɔji lɛ amɛkɛɛ, "Nyɛwekunyo ko egbo."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The birds came and saw that it was Ajao. They said, "This animal is not part of our family."
ga: Loofɔji lɛ ba ni amɛbana akɛ Ajao ni. Amɛkɛɛ, "Kooloo nɛɛ fataaa wɔweku lɛ he."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: "All our family have feathers but Ajao has none. So, he is not one of us." The birds went away.
ga: "Wɔweku nɛɛ mli mɛi fɛɛ yɛ tsɛji. Ajao bɛ eko. Hewɔ lɛ, jeee wɔteŋ mɔ kome ni."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The neighbours reasoned together. They agreed, "The birds are right. Ajao has no feathers. So, he is not their relative."
ga: Henɔi lɛ susu sane lɛ he. Amɛkpã gbee amɛkɛɛ, "Loofɔji lɛ asane ja. Ajao bɛ tsɛji. Hewɔ lɛ, jeee amɛwekunyo ji Ajao."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: One of them said, "He must be part of the family of rats. He looks like them."
ga: Henɔi lɛ ateŋ mɔ kome kɛɛ, "Ajao baafee obishii lɛ awekunyo. Eje amɛ."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The neighbours went and called the rats saying, "One of your family is dead."
ga: Henɔi lɛ tee amɛyatsɛ obishii lɛ amɛkɛɛ, "Nyɛwekunyo ko egbo."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: The rats came and saw that it was Ajao. They said, "This animal is not part of our family."
ga: Obishii lɛ ba ni amɛbana akɛ Ajao ni. Amɛkɛɛ, "Kooloo nɛɛ egbeee wɔweku lɛ yi."
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: "Everyone in our family has a tail. Ajao has no tail." The rats went away.
ga: Wɔweku nɛɛ mli mɔ fɛɛ mɔ yɛ lei. Ajao bɛ lei." Obishii lɛ hu tee.
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: No relations were found for Ajao and he remained unburied.
ga: Anaaa mɛi pɔtɛɛ ni ji Ajao webii. Enɛ hewɔ anaaa afũ Ajao lɛ.
title: Why Ajao was not buried
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Taiwo Ẹhinẹni, Ga translation by Aisha Nelson, illustrations by Jesse Breytenbach

english: Clever Nomusa
ga: Nomusa ni yɔɔ nilee
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: In Masoyi village, there was a very clever girl called Nomusa. She lived with her grandmother, who was a maize farmer. Most of the people in the village could not read or write. They made their living from farming.
ga: Yɛ Masoyi akrowa lɛ mli lɛ, gbekɛ yoo ko ni le nii waa yɛ ni atsɛɔ lɛ Nomusa. Ekɛ enaa, ni ji ŋmãa okwaafonyo lɛ hi shi. Mɛi ni yɔɔ akrowa lɛ mli lɛ ateŋ mɛi babaoo leee nikanemɔ loo niŋmaa. Amɛyeɔ amɛshihilɛ kɛjɛɔ okwaayeli mli.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Nomusa liked attending school, and her grandmother was proud of her. Each day after school, her grandmother gave her chores on the farm. She had to chase the monkeys and birds that wanted to eat the crops.
ga: Nomusa sumɔɔ skul yaa, ni enaa kɛ ehe fɔ̃ɔ enɔ. Daa gbi kɛjɛ skul lɛ, enaa haa lɛ shĩa nitsumɔi yɛ ŋmɔ lɛ mli. Ehe bahia ni etiu ŋmeii kɛ okpoi ni miisumɔ ni amɛye ŋmɔshi nibii lɛ.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Nomusa found it difficult to chase monkeys and birds all afternoon. She often did not have time to complete her schoolwork. Many children in the village missed school altogether because they had to work in the fields.
ga: Ewa kɛha Nomusa akɛ ebaatiu ŋmeii kɛ okpoi shwane muu lɛ fɛɛ. Bei pii lɛ, enáaa be ni ekɛbaagbe e-skul nitsumɔi lɛ anaa. Gbekɛbii babaoo ni yɔɔ akrowa lɛ mli lɛ eyaaa skul kwraa ejaakɛ esa akɛ amɛtsu nii yɛ ŋmɔ mli.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: As time passed, Nomusa grew more and more tired of chasing birds and monkeys. “I have a good idea,” she thought.
ga: Beni bei hoɔ lɛ, Nomusa he jɔ̃ ehe waa yɛ okpoi kɛ ŋmeii asɛɛtiumɔ he. Esusu akɛ, "Miyɛ susumɔ kpakpa ko."
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Nomusa carefully tied two long sticks together. She dressed the sticks in her work clothes. She held the sticks upright and put her work hat on top. It was a scarecrow!
ga: Nomusa fimɔ tsei kakadaji enyɔ jogbaŋŋ. Ekɛ enitsumɔ atadei lɛ wo tsei lɛ amli. Ehiɛ tsei lɛ amli shiŋŋ ni ekɛ enitsumɔ tsɔne lɛ wo nɔ. Eji gbeyeishemɔ ko!
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Nomusa put the scarecrow in the middle of the maize field. “This scarecrow will take my place while I do schoolwork. Grandmother will think I am in the field,” Nomusa smiled to herself.
ga: Nomusa kɛ gbeyeishemɔ lɛ wo ŋmãa ŋmɔ lɛ teŋgbɛ. "Nɛkɛ gbeyeishemɔ nɛɛ baaye mi najiaŋ be mli ni mitsuɔ skul nitsumɔi. Nana baasusu akɛ miyɛ ŋmɔ mli," Nomusa ŋmɔ kɛ ehe.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Each day, she took her school bag to the field. She stayed in her school uniform and put her work clothes on the scarecrow. Then, she did her homework in the shade of a tree.
ga: Daa gbi lɛ, ekɛ e-skul kotoku lɛ yaa ŋmɔ mli. Ehi e-skul atade lɛ mli ni ekɛ enitsumɔ atadei lɛ wo gbeyeishemɔ tsɔne lɛ nɔ. Kɛkɛ lɛ, efee eshia nitsumɔ yɛ tso ko shishi.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Days went by and Nomusa thought, “Grandmother will never find out about my clever plan.” Nomusa was happy and surprised at the same time. The monkeys and birds didn’t go into the maize field.
ga: Gbii ho ni Nomusa susu akɛ, "Nana lɛ enaŋ mi gbɛjianɔtoo ni yɔɔ ŋaa lɛ he sane kɔkɔɔkɔ." Nomusa miishɛɛ ni enaa kpɛ ehe yɛ nakai beaŋ nɔŋŋ. Akpɔlɔi kɛ okpoi lɛ eyaaa ŋmãa ŋmɔ lɛ mli.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: One afternoon, Nomusa’s grandmother went to the field to get fresh mealies. The field was very quiet. There were no monkeys or birds anywhere. Grandmother thought to herself, “Nomusa is doing a good job.”
ga: Gbi ko shwane lɛ, Nomusa nanaa tee ŋmɔ lɛ mli koni eyahe niyenii hee. Gbo lɛ mli fee dioo waa. No mli lɛ, ŋmeii loo okpoi bɛ he ko he ko. Nana susu yɛ ehe akɛ, "Nomusa miitsu nitsumɔ kpakpa."
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Grandmother called out, “Nomusa! Nomusa! Where are you?” There was no response. Then she saw the scarecrow in the middle of the field, wearing Nomusa’s clothes!
ga: Nana tsɛ lɛ akɛ, "Nomusa! Nomusa! Nɛgbɛ oyɔɔ?" Hetoo ko bɛ. Kɛkɛ ni ena gbeyeishemɔ lɛ yɛ ŋmɔ lɛ teŋgbɛ, ni ewo Nomusa atadei!
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: When grandmother realised what Nomusa had done, she was proud of her granddaughter. She thought, “This is very clever. Nomusa doesn’t have to go into the field to chase the monkeys and birds away.”
ga: Beni enaa lɛ yɔse nɔ ni Nomusa fee lɛ, ekɛ enaa lɛ wo ehe nɔ. Esusu akɛ, "Enɛ ji nilee waa. Ehe ehiaaa ni Nomusa aya ŋmɔ mli koni eyashwie akpɔlɔi kɛ okpoi lɛ."
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Everyone in the village loved Nomusa’s clever idea. They all started using scarecrows on their farms. The scarecrows kept the monkeys and birds away from the fields. And the children could go to school instead of looking after crops.
ga: Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ ni yɔɔ akrowa lɛ mli lɛ sumɔɔ Nomusa ŋaa susumɔ lɛ. Amɛ fɛɛ amɛbɔi ŋmeii kɛ nitsumɔ yɛ amɛŋmɔji amli. Gbeyei ni gbeɔ mɔ lɛ haa ŋmeii kɛ okpoi lɛ tsiɔ amɛhe kɛjɛɔ ŋmɔji lɛ ahe. Ni gbekɛbii lɛ baanyɛ aya skul moŋ fe ni amɛaakwɛ ŋmɔshi nibii anɔ.
title: Clever Nomusa
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Zandile Malaza, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Simon Mokoena

english: Man with a serious problem
ga: Nuu ni hiɛ naagba ko ni mli wa
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: Mandu lived with his grandparents, his aunt and an uncle. He had a hen, a goat, a sheep and a pig. The hen stayed in a small cage. The goat, sheep and pig were each tied on the side of the wall. The grandparents were still well. The aunt and uncle helped with the work.
ga: Mandu kɛ enaa, enii, enyɛkwɛ̃ kɛ etsɛkwɛ̃ ko hi shi. Eyɛ kooloo, wuɔ, too abotia, too gwantɛi kɛ kpootoo. wuɔ lɛ hi tsũ bibioo ko mli. Akɛ too abotia , too gwantɛi kɛ kpootoo lɛ fĩ gbogbo lɛ he. No mli lɛ, enaa kɛ enii lɛ he wa lolo. Nyɛkwɛ kɛ tsɛkwɛ̃ ye amɛbua yɛ nitsumɔ lɛ mli.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: This changed few years later. Mandu's grandparents aged and could not hear or see well. His aunt became sickly and could not help clean the house. His uncle slept all the time and did not help to feed the animals.
ga: Enɛ tsake yɛ afii fioo komɛi asɛɛ. Mandu naa kɛ enii edara ni amɛnuuu nii loo amɛnaaa nii jogbaŋŋ. Hela mɔ enyɛkwɛ̃ lɛ ni enyɛɛɛ eye ebua ni asaa shia lɛ mli. Etsɛkwɛ̃ lɛ wɔɔ be fɛɛ be ni eyeee ebuaaa kooloi lɛ niyenii.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: The animals made so much noise because they were hungry. The house was so dirty because the aunt did not clean it. Mandu was tired all the time. He had to go out every day to look for food for them all.
ga: Koolooi lɛ fee hoo waa ejaakɛ hɔmɔ miiye amɛ. Shĩa lɛ mli ewo muji waa ejaakɛ enyɛkwɛ̃ lɛ esaaa jɛi. Etɔ Mandu be fɛɛ be. Ehe bahia ni eje kpo daa gbi koni eyatao niyenii eha amɛ fɛɛ.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: Mandu could not cope with the situation anymore. He asked his elderly grandparents for a solution. He was unhappy because his grandparents did not hear him. His sick aunt said, "All I want is to be able to sleep at night and wake up in the morning."
ga: Mandu nyɛɛɛ adamɔ shihilɛ lɛ naa dɔŋŋ. Ebi enaamɛi ni edara lɛ koni amɛha lɛ tsabaa. Emii shɛɛɛ ehe ejaakɛ enaamɛi nuuu lɛ toi. Etsɛkwɛ̃ ni hela mɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Nɔ pɛ ni misumɔɔ ji ni manyɛ mawɔ gbɛkɛ ni mate shi leebi."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: His lazy uncle said, "Sell the animals and buy food for your grandparents. They will sleep and won't bother you." Mandu was angry. He said, "Uncle, you know that I cannot sell the animals. They are the only wealth I have."
ga: Etsɛkwɛ̃ ni bɛ jwɛŋmɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Hɔɔ kooloi lɛ ni ohé niyenii oha onanamɛi. Amɛbaawɔ ni amɛgbaŋ bo naa." Mandu mli fu. Ekɛɛ, "Tsɛkwɛ, ole akɛ minyɛɛɛ mahɔ̃ɔ kooloi lɛ. Amɛ pɛ ji ninamɔ ni miyɔɔ."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: One night Mandu lay awake. He remembered a wise man who was believed to have solutions to all problems. Mandu took his animals and visited the wise man. He kept a rope on the goat, sheep and pig and carried the hen.
ga: Gbi ko gbɛkɛ lɛ, Mandu kã shi. Ekai nilelɔ ko ni aheɔ ayeɔ akɛ eyɛ naagbai fɛɛ anaa tsabaa lɛ. Mandu kɛ ekooloi lɛ tee ni amɛyasara nilelɔ lɛ. Ekɛ kpã fɔ̃ɔ too, too kɛ kpootoo nɔ ni ewoɔ kooloo lɛ.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: Mandu arrived at the wise man's home, tired and hungry. After explaining his problem to the wise man, the wise man said, "I will help you but you must do as I say." Mandu replied, "I will do anything to solve my problem."
ga: Mandu yashɛ nilelɔ lɛ shia, ni etɔ lɛ ni hɔmɔ hu miiye lɛ. Beni nilelɔ lɛ gbala enaagba lɛ mli etsɔɔ nilelɔ lɛ sɛɛ lɛ, ekɛɛ, "Maye mabua bo shi esa akɛ ofee bɔ ni mikɛɔ lɛ." Mandu ha hetoo akɛ, "Mafee nɔ fɛɛ nɔ koni matsu minaagba lɛ he nii."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: The wise man said, "Leave the animals here and go back to your house." Mandu said, "But I have lived with my animals for a long time. They are the only wealth I have."
ga: Nilelɔ lɛ kɛɛ akɛ, "Shi kooloi lɛ yɛ biɛ ni oya oshia." Mandu kɛɛ, "Shi mikɛ mi kooloi lɛ ehi shi be kakadaŋŋ. Amɛ pɛ ji ninamɔ ni miyɔɔ."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: The wise man said, "I told you I would help you but you must do as I say." Mandu needed a solution to his problem. He left his animals and returned home.
ga: Nileelɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Mikɛɛ bo akɛ maye mabua bo shi esa akɛ ofee bɔ ni mikɛɔ lɛ." Ehe miihia ni Mandu ana enaagba lɛ naa tsabaa. Eshi ekooloi lɛ ni eku esɛɛ kɛtee shĩa.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: His house was too quiet and empty. Everybody missed the animals. Mandu's grandparents complained because they had no milk from the goat. The uncle said, "We are so poor, everyone is laughing at us."
ga: Eshia lɛ mli efee dioo tsɔ ni nɔ ko bɛ mli. Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ hiɛ kpa koolooi lɛ anɔ. Mandu naa kɛ nii wie huhuuhu ejaakɛ amɛbɛ too lɛ fufɔ mli nu. Tsɛkwɛ lɛ kɛɛ, "Wɔye ohia waa, mɔ fɛɛ mɔ miiŋmɔ wɔ."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: Mandu could not cope with the complaints anymore. Besides, he missed his animals too. He returned to the wise man to ask for advice. "Life is very different without my animals in the house. My relatives miss them too much."
ga: Mandu nyɛɛɛ akpee huhuuhu wiemɔi lɛ anaa dɔŋŋ. Kɛfata he lɛ, ehiɛ kpa ekooloi lɛ hu anɔ. Eku esɛɛ kɛtee nilelɔ lɛ ŋɔɔ koni eyabi lɛ ŋaawoo. "Shihilɛ yɛ srɔto kwraa kɛji mi kooloi bɛ shĩa. Miwekumɛi lɛ ahiɛ kpaa amɛnɔ waa."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: The wise man said, "I will help you but you must do as I tell you. Go home and take your grandparents out of the house." Mandu said, "How can I do that? They are my grandparents and they depend on me."
ga: Nilelɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Maye mabua bo shi esa akɛ ofee bɔ ni mikɛɛ bo lɛ. Yaa shia ni oyajie onanamɛi kɛjɛ shia." Mandu kɛɛ, "Te mafee tɛŋŋ mafee nakai? Amɛji minaa kɛ minii ni hiɛ ka minɔ."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: In the end, Mandu went home and did as he was told. He did not have any peace of mind. His grandparents had nowhere to go. They wandered around, trying not to bump into things. They felt the heat during the day and the cold at night.
ga: Yɛ naagbee lɛ, Mandu tee shia ni eyafee bɔ ni akɛɛ lɛ lɛ. Ebɛ jwɛŋmɔŋ toiŋjɔlɛ ko kwraa. Enaa kɛ enii bɛ he ko ni amɛbaaya. Amɛbɔle amɛhe, ni amɛmiitao ni amɛkɛ nibii akakpe. Amɛnu dɔlɛ he yɛ shwane mli, ni amɛnu fɛ̃i he gbɛkɛ.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: His sick aunt cried, "Don't throw me out!" His lazy uncle cried, "Don't throw me out either!"
ga: Enyɛkwɛ̃ ni bɛ hewalɛ lɛ fo akɛ, "Kaashwie mi kɛje kpo!" Etsɛkwɛ̃ anihaolɔ lɛ bolɔ akɛ, "Kaashwie mi hu!"
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: Mandu could not take it anymore. He returned to the wise man confused and angry. He cried saying, "This is too much for one person. Give me a better solution."
ga: Mandu nyɛɛɛ ekɛtsu nii dɔŋŋ. Eku esɛɛ kɛtee nilelɔ lɛ ŋɔɔ ni eyiŋ efutu lɛ ni emli efu. Efo ni ekɛɛ, "Enɛ fa tsɔ kɛha mɔ kome. Ha mi tsabaa kpakpa."
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

english: The wise man said, "Here, take your animals home and return your grandparents in the house." Mandu did as he was told. His aunt said, "I will clean the house." His uncle stopped being lazy and helped Mandu with work. They were all happy once more.
ga: Nileelɔ lɛ kɛɛ, "Naa, okɛ okooloi lɛ aya shia ni okɛ onanamɛi aku sɛɛ kɛba shia." Mandu fee bɔ ni akɛɛ lɛ lɛ. Etsɛkwɛ̃ kɛɛ, "Matsumɔ shĩa lɛ mli." Etsɛkwɛ̃ kpa anihaofeemɔ ni eye ebua Mandu kɛ nitsumɔ. Amɛ fɛɛ amɛmii shɛ amɛhe shikome ekoŋŋ.
title: Man with a serious problem
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Abraham Muzee

ga: Moi haa Pendo yakpeɔ jwɛi kɛji ekpa skul.

source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

title: Pendo, our cow
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

ga: Pendo haa fufɔ mli nu pii.
title: Pendo, our cow
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

ga: Tsɛ ataa hɔɔ Pendo fufɔ mli nu lɛ.
title: Pendo, our cow
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen
