ga: Moi nuɔ fufɔ mli nu daa gbi.
title: Pendo, our cow
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

ga: Ekɛɛ, "Pendo Oyiwaladɔŋŋ!"
title: Pendo, our cow
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Ruth Odondi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald, Rob Owen

english: Greedy Kiundu
ga: Saki Hiɛjoolɔ
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: A long time ago, in the village of Nyamani, there lived a man known as Kiundu. Kiundu liked to eat very much. He especially liked to eat meat.
ga: Be ko in eho jeeŋmɔ lɛ, nuu ko ni atsɛɔ lɛ Saki hi shi yɛ Kweimaŋ. Eyeɔ ŋmaa naakpa. Esumɔɔ milɛ loo titri.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: One day, the chief of the village invited all the villagers to his son's wedding.
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, akrowa lɛ mli maŋtsɛ lɛ fɔ nine kɛtsɛ akrowa lɛ mli bii lɛ fɛɛ kɛba ebinuu lɛ yookpeemɔ.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Then Kiundu heard people talking about another wedding party. It was in a nearby village called Katumbi. "Two parties on the same day!" Kiundu thought.
ga: Saki nu ni mɛi komɛi miiwie akɛ ayɛ yookpeemɔ paati kroko ko hu yɛ akrowa nitsa amɛ nɔ ni atsɛɔ lɛ Adomaŋ lɛ. "Paatii enyɔ yɛ gbi kome nɔ!" Saki jwɛŋ he.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: "I must attend both parties," Kiundu said to himself. "I will first walk to Katumbi and then come back to Nyamani."
ga: "Esani maya enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ," Saki kɛɛ ehe. Klɛŋklɛŋ lɛ, manyiɛ kɛya Adomaŋ kɛkɛ lɛ miku misɛɛ kɛba Kweimaŋ.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Kiundu woke up early in the morning and walked to Katumbi village. When he arrived he saw that the cooks were still preparing the food. "I will go back to Nyamani and return here later," Kiundu decided.
ga: Saki te shi leebi maŋkpa ni enyiɛ kɛtee Adomaŋ akroma lɛ mli. Be ni eshɛ jɛmɛ lɛ, ena akɛ nihoolɔi lɛ miihoo niyenii lɛ lolo. "Maku misɛɛ kɛya Kweimaŋ ni maba be kroko," Saki fee eyiŋ.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Kiundu walked back to Nyamani hoping to find the meat ready. He was now hungry. But when he arrived, people there were also still preparing the food.
ga: Saki nyiɛ kɛtee Kweimaŋ ekoŋŋ belɛ eekpa gbɛ akɛ milɛ loo lɛ baabe. Agbɛnɛ hɔmɔ miiye lɛ. Shi be ni eshɛ jɛmɛ lɛ, jɛmɛ nihoolɔi lɛ hu miihoo niyenii lɛ loloolo.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: "When I left Katumbi they were starting to cook," he thought. "The food must be ready now." So Kiundu walked back to Katumbi. He was now very hungry.
ga: Ekɛɛ yɛ eyiŋ akɛ, "Be ni mishi Adomaŋ lɛ amɛmiije niyenii lɛ hoomɔ lɛ shishi. Be nɛɛ lɛ ebe." Hewɔ lɛ, Saki nyiɛ ekoŋŋ kɛtee Adomaŋ. Agbɛnɛ, hɔmɔ miiye lɛ jeee shwɛmɔ.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: By the time Kiundu got to Katumbi, people had already eaten. Guests were giving presents to the bride and the groom. Kiundu did not have a gift to give. He only wanted to eat.
ga: Be ni Saki shɛ Adomaŋ lɛ gbɔmɛi lɛ eye niyenii lɛ momo. Gbɔi lɛ miike ayɛmfro kɛ ayɛmfrowu lɛ nibii. Saki bɛ nikee ko. Niyenii pɛ etaoɔ ni eye.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Kiundu was most disappointed about missing the food. He decided to walk back to Nyamani village. He was hungry and tired and walked very slowly.
ga: Edɔ Saki jogbaŋŋ akɛ aye niyenii lɛ ashi lɛ. Efee eyiŋ akɛ ebaaku esɛɛ kɛya Kweimaŋ akrowa lɛ mli ekoŋŋ. Akɛni etɔ lɛ ni hɔmɔ hu miiye lɛ hewɔ lɛ, enyiɛ blɛoo.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: When he arrived at Nyamani village, people were singing and dancing. They had already eaten all the food!
ga: Be ni eshɛ Kweimaŋ akrowa lɛ mli lɛ, gbɔmɛi lɛ miila ni aajo. Amɛye niyenii lɛ fɛɛ momo!
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: When he heard that there was no food, Kiundu fainted. He had missed meat from both parties. When he recovered, he got some porridge in a small cup!
ga: Be ni Saki nu akɛ niyenii bɛ lɛ, nɔ nyɔ enɔ. Enaaa loo yɛ paatii enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ. Be ni ehiɛtsɛ lɛ, aha lɛ akasa yɛ kɔɔpoo bibioo ko mli.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Kiundu walked home again, still hungry.
ga: Saki nyiɛ kɛtee shia ekoŋŋ kɛ hɔmɔ.
title: Greedy Kiundu
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Mutugi Kamundi, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Zablon Alex Nguku

english: Sara's Canoe
ga: Sara Lɛlɛ lɛ
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Sara has a canoe. Her canoe is big. It is by the riverside.
ga: Sara yɛ lɛlɛ. Elɛlɛ lɛ da. Ema faa lɛ naa.
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Some women come to the river. One woman has a basin of fruit. Another woman has a chicken. Another woman has a goat. Another woman has two goats. They ask Sara, "How can we get to the other side of the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!"
ga: Yei komɛi ba faa lɛ naa. Mᴐ kome hiɛ gagba ni aduawai yɛ mli. Yoo kroko hu hiɛ wuᴐ. Mᴐ kroko hu hiɛ too abotia. Ni Mᴐ kroko hu hiɛ abotiai enyᴐ. Amɛ bi Sara akɛ, "Te wᴐbaafee tɛŋŋ wᴐyashɛ faa lɛ sɛɛ?" Sara kɛɛ, "Nyɛ botea milɛlɛ lɛ mli!"
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Then, some men arrive. One man has a fish. Another man has a bicycle. Another man has a sack of maize.
ga: No mli nᴐŋŋ ni hii komɛi hu bashɛ shi. Hii lɛ ateŋ mᴐ kome hiɛ loo. Mᴐ kome hu hiɛ okᴐᴐkpe. Mᴐ kroko hu hiɛ abele kɛ kotoku.
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Another man has two sacks of maize. They ask Sara, "How can we get to the other side of the river?" Sara replies, "Get in my canoe!"
ga: Nuu kroko hu hiɛ abele kɛ kotokui enyᴐ. Amɛ bi Sara akɛ, "Te wᴐbaafee tɛŋŋ ni wᴐyashɛ faa lɛ sɛɛ?" Sara here nᴐ ekɛɛ, "Nyɛ botea milɛlɛ lɛ mli!"
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Some animals come to the river. They ask Sara, "How can we get across the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!"
ga: Kooloi komɛi ba faa lɛ naa. Amɛ bi Sara akɛ, "Te wᴐbaafee tɛŋŋ wᴐbaafo faa lɛ?" Sara kɛɛ, "Nyɛ botea milɛlɛ lɛ mli!"
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: The animals get in the canoe. The dog gets in the canoe. The cat gets in the canoe. The monkey gets in the canoe. The rabbit gets in the canoe. The turtle gets in the canoe. The gazelle gets in the canoe.
ga: Kooloi lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Gbee lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Alᴐŋte lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Aduŋ lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Kpɛŋkpɛ̃lɛ̃ lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Gosaŋe lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Baayelᴐ lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli.
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: The elephant arrives at the river. He asks, "How can I get to the other side of the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!" The elephant gets in the canoe. The canoe fills up with water.
ga: Shwuᴐ hu bashɛ faa lɛ naa. Ebi akɛ, "Te mafee tɛŋŋ ni mashɛ faa lɛ sɛɛ?" Sara kɛɛ, "Botemᴐ milɛlɛ lɛ mli!" Shwuᴐ lɛ bote lɛlɛ lɛ mli. Lɛlɛ lɛ yi kɛ nu.
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: The canoe is too small. There isn't enough room.
ga: Lɛlɛ lɛ yɛ bibioo tsᴐ. Gbɛ faa yɛ mli nakai.
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Sara says, "Hold on! First I'll take the women."
ga: Sara kɛɛ, "Nyɛ mɛa! Klɛŋklɛŋ lɛ, mi kɛ yei lɛ baaya."
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Sara says, "Second, I'll take the men."
ga: Sara kɛɛ, "No sɛɛ lɛ, mawo hii lɛ kɛya."
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Sara says, "Finally, I'll take the animals."
ga: Sara kɛɛ, "Naagbee kwraa lɛ, mawo kooloi lɛ."
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: The elephant says, "I'm just going to walk!"
ga: Shwuᴐ lɛ kɛɛ, "Mi lɛ manyiɛ moŋ kɛkɛ!"
title: Sara's Canoe
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Little Zebra Books, Ga translation by Ezekiel Johnson, illustrations by Rachel Greer

english: Holidays with grandmother
ga: Sowa Kɛ Laye Yasara Amɛ Naa
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Odongo and Apiyo lived in the city with their father. They looked forward to the holidays. Not only because school was closed, but because they went to visit their grandmother. She lived in a fishing village near a large lake.
ga: Sowa kɛ Laye kɛ amɛ tsɛ ataa hi shi yɛ maŋ ko mli. Amɛkpa gbɛ akɛ aha skul gbɛ koni amɛyasara amɛ naa. Ehi akrowa ko ni bɛŋkɛ kpaakpo agbo ko he.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Odongo and Apiyo were excited because it was time to visit their grandmother again. They packed their bags and got ready for their long journey the next day. They could not sleep and talked about the holiday the whole night.
ga: Sowa kɛ Laye miishɛ amɛhe ejaakɛ be eshɛ kɛha amɛnaa saramɔ ekoŋŋ. Gbɛkɛ dani je baatsɛre kɛha amɛgbɛfaa lɛ, amɛto amɛ nibii fɛɛ kɛwo amɛ bagii amli ni amɛsaa amɛhe kɛha gbɛfaa kakadaŋŋ lɛ. Nakai gbɛkɛ lɛ, amɛ wɔɔɔ. Amɛgba gbijurɔ lɛ he sane aahu.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: After a while, the children were tired and fell asleep.
ga: Be ni jetsɛre leebi maŋkpa lɛ, amɛshi kɛtee akrowa lɛ mli kɛ amɛtsɛ ataa tsɔne lɛ. Be ni amɛyaa yɛ gbɛjegbɛ lɛ nɔ lɛ, amɛtsɔne lɛho gɔji, kooloi kɛ ŋmɔji komɛi ahe. Amɛkane tsɔji ni amɛla lalai. Be saŋŋ sɛɛ lɛ, etɔ gbekɛbii lɛ hewɔ lɛ amɛkamɔshi ni amɛwɔ yɛ tsɔne lɛ mli.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Father woke up Odongo and Apiyo as they arrived in the village. They found Nyar-Kanyada, their grandmother, resting on a mat under a tree. In thier language, Nyar-Kanyada means "daughter of the people of Kanyada." She was a strong and beautiful woman.
ga: Tsɛ ataa tsiɛ Sowa kɛ Laye be ni amɛshɛ akrowa lɛ mli lɛ. Amɛna amɛnaa, Naa Momo ka saa ko nɔ yɛ tso ko shishi ni eejɔɔ ehe.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Nyar-Kanyada welcomed them into the house. She danced around the room singing with joy. Her grandchildren were excited to give her the presents they brought from the city. "First open my gift," said Odongo. "No, my gift first!" said Apiyo.
ga: Naa Momo kɛ lala kɛ joo nya amɛhe kɛbote shia lɛ mli. Enabii lɛ kɛ miishɛɛ ha lɛ nikee nibii ni amɛkɛba lɛ. "Gbelemɔ minikee lɛ naa klɛŋklɛŋ," Sowa kɛɛ. "Dabi, minɔ lɛ klɛŋklɛŋ," Laye kɛɛ.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: After she opened the presents, Nyar-Kanyada blessed her grandchildren in a traditional way.
ga: Be ni Naa Momo gbele nibii lɛ anaa lɛ, ejɔɔ enabii lɛ. Kɛkɛ ni Sowa kɛ Laye jekpo kɛtee agbo lɛ naa amɛyashwɛ. Naa Momo kɛ ebinuu lɛ gba amɛweku lɛ he sane kɛ jeŋ saji komɛi ahe sane.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: When it was dark they returned to the house for dinner. Before they could finish eating, they were falling asleep!
ga: Be ni duŋ wo lɛ, Sowa kɛ Laye ku amɛsɛɛ kɛtee shia lɛ mli ni amɛyaye gbɛkɛ niyenii. Amɛgbeee niyeli lɛ naa ni wɔnyɔmɔ amɛ nɔ! Ni je tsɛre lɛ, gbekɛbii lɛ atsɛ ataa shi amɛ yɛ Naa Momo ŋɔ ni etee maŋ wulu lɛ mli.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Odongo and Apiyo helped their grandmother with household chores. They fetched water and firewood. They collected eggs from the chickens and picked vegetables from the garden.
ga: Sowa kɛ Laye ye bua amɛ naa kɛ shia nitsumɔ. Amɛfo nu ni amɛ lɛ lai. Amɛya kɔlɔ wɔji yɛ wuɔi lɛ ashishi ni amɛtserɛ yelibai yɛ abɔɔ lɛ mli.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: One morning, Odongo took his grandmother's cows to graze. They ran onto a neighbour's farm. The farmer was angry with Odongo. He threatened to keep the cows for eating his crops. After that day, the boy made sure that the cows did not get into trouble again.
ga: Leebi ko lɛ, Sowa kɛ enaa tsina yei lɛ tee jwɛikpemɔ. Amɛjo foi kɛtee ŋmɔ ko ni bɛŋkɛ amɛ mli. Okwaafonyo lɛ mli fu. Eto eyiŋ akɛ ebaatsi tsinai lɛ anaa ejaakɛ amɛye eŋmɔshi nibii lɛ. Kɛjɛ nakai gbi lɛ, Sowa bɔɔ mɔdeŋ akɛ tsinai lɛ yataooo sane kɛbaaa dɔŋŋ.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: On another day, the children went to the market place with Nyar-Kanyada. She had a stall selling vegetables, sugar and soap. Apiyo liked to tell customers the price of items. Odongo would pack the items that customers bought.
ga: Gbi kroko lɛ, Naa Momo kɛ gbekɛbii lɛ tee jara lɛ nɔ. Eyɛ agba ko ni ehɔɔ yelibai, sikli kɛ samala yɛ mli. Laye sumɔɔ ni etsɔɔ nihelɔi lɛ nibii lɛ ajara. Sowa baato nibii ni nihelɔi lɛ he lɛ kɛhaa amɛ.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: But too soon the holidays were over. The children had to go back to the city. Nyar-Kanyada gave Odongo a cap and Apiyo a sweater. She packed food for their journey.
ga: Gbɛhamɔ be lɛ eba naagbee. Esa ni gbekɛbii lɛ aku amɛsɛɛ kɛya skul yɛ maŋ wulu lɛ mli. Naa Mono ha Sowa fai ni eha Laye Suwɛta. Eto niyenii kɛha amɛgbɛfaa lɛ.
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: When their father came to fetch them, they did not want to leave. The children begged Nyar-Kanyada to go with them to the city. She smiled and said, "I am too old for the city. I will be waiting for you to visit me again."
ga: Be ni amɛtsɛ ataa ba amɛwolemɔ lɛ, amɛ sumɔɔ ni amɛyaa. Gbekɛbii lɛ kpa Naa Momo fai koni efata amɛhe kɛya maŋ wulu lɛ mli. Eŋmɔ mugɛɛ ni ekɛɛ, "Migbɔ fe maŋ wulu mli shihilɛ. Mamɛ nyɛ yɛ biɛ koni wɔsɛɛ skul gbɛhamɔ lɛ hu nyɛbasara mi."
title: Holidays with grandmother
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Violet Otieno, Ga translation by Divine Apedo (OLE Ghana), illustrations by Catherine Groenewald

english: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
ga: Thakgalo lala he helatsɛmɛi ashwiili lɛ
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Thakgalo means happiness. Thakgalo is a person who uses a wheelchair. Her family and friends love her so much.
ga: Thakgalo shishi ji miishɛɛ. Thakgalo ji mɔ ko ni kɛ helatsɛmɛi ashwiili tsuɔ nii. Ewekumɛi kɛ enanemɛi sumɔɔ lɛ waa.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Thakgalo loves music. Her friends love dancing and playing music for her.
ga: Thakgalo sumɔɔ lala waa. Enanemɛi lɛ sumɔɔ joo kɛ lalai ni amɛtswaa amɛhaa lɛ.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Her friends installed a musical speaker on Thakgalo's wheelchair. When she touched a button on one side of the wheelchair, music would play.
ga: Enanemɛi lɛ kɛ lala he wiemɔ tsɔne ko wo Thakgalo helatsɛmɛi ashwiili lɛ nɔ. Kɛ́ eta bɔtin ko ni yɔɔ helatsɛmɛi ashwiili lɛ fã kome lɛ he lɛ, lala tswaa.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Thakgalo would stretch herself and dance to the musical wheelchair. She practised dancing on her own, and then began to dance with her friends.
ga: Thakgalo baajie ehe ni ejo kɛya lala he helatsɛmɛi ashwiili lɛ nɔ. Ekase joo lɛ diɛŋtsɛ, ni no sɛɛ lɛ ekɛ enanemɛi lɛ bɔi joo.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: One day her friends saw a dance competition advertised in the newspaper. They asked Thakgalo's mom if they could enter the competition for her. Thakgalo's mom agreed.
ga: Gbi ko lɛ, enanemɛi lɛ na joo he akaŋshii ko ni atswa he adafi yɛ adafitswaa wolo mli. Amɛbi Thakgalo nyɛ kɛji amɛbaanyɛ amɛbote akaŋshii lɛ mli amɛha lɛ. Thakgalo nyɛ kpɛlɛ nɔ.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Thakgalo's friends borrowed her mom's cell phone to make a video for the dance competition. They videoed Thakgalo dancing to her favourite song, then they sent the video entry to the competition. Thakgalo was chosen for the competition!
ga: Thakgalo nanemɛi lɛ fa emami tɛlifoŋ lɛ koni amɛkɛfee vidio kɛha joo he akaŋshii lɛ. Amɛjie Thakgalo lala ni esumɔɔ waa lɛ joɔ lɛ he vidio, kɛkɛ ni amɛkɛ vidio lɛ mlibotemɔ lɛ maje akaŋshii lɛ. Ahala Thakgalo kɛha akaŋshii lɛ!
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: The competition day arrived. Thakgalo wore a beautiful new outfit. When the music played, she moved gracefully and with joy.
ga: Akaŋshii gbi lɛ bashɛ. Thakgalo wo atade hee fɛfɛo ko. Kɛ́ lala lɛ tswa lɛ, ekɛ miishɛɛ tsiɔ ehe kɛyaa kɛbaa.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: People in the audience shouted her name, "Thakgalo! Thakgalo!" Truly, she was the dancing star of the day. Thakgalo won the competition and many prizes.
ga: Mɛi ni yɔɔ toibolɔi lɛ ateŋ lɛ bolɔ amɛtsɛ egbɛi, "Thakgalo! Thakgalo!" Anɔkwale, lɛ ji ŋulami ni joɔ yɛ nakai gbi lɛ mli. Thakgalo ye kunim yɛ akaŋshii lɛ mli kɛ jweremɔ nii babaoo.
title: Thakgalo's musical wheelchair
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Diana Tebeila, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Diana Tebeila

english: Tom the banana seller
ga: Tom ni ji akwadu hɔlɔlɔ lɛ
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Tom carries a tray of ripe bananas.
ga: Tom hiɛ akwadu ni etsu.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Tom goes to the market to sell bananas.
ga: Tom yaa jara nɔ koni eyahɔ̃ɔ akwadu.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: People at the market are buying fruit.
ga: Mɛi ni yɔɔ jara lɛ nɔ lɛ miihe aduawai.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: But no one is buying Tom's bananas. They prefer to buy fruit from women.
ga: Shi mɔ ko mɔ ko heee Tom akwadu lɛ. Amɛsumɔɔ ni amɛhe aduawai kɛjɛ yei adɛŋ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: "In our community, only women sell fruit," people say. "What kind of a man is this?" people ask.
ga: "Yɛ wɔ akutso lɛ mli lɛ, yei pɛ hɔ̃ɔ aduawai," mɛi kɛɔ. "Mɛɛ gbɔmɔ ji mɔ nɛɛ?" mɛi biɔ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: But Tom does not give up. He calls, "Buy my bananas! Buy my sweet ripe bananas!"
ga: Shi Tom nijiaŋ ejeee wui. Etsɛɔ, "Hɔɔ mi akwadu! Hemɔ mi akwadu ni egbɔ ni ŋɔɔ!"
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: One woman picks up a bunch of bananas from the tray. She looks at the bananas carefully.
ga: Yoo ko holeɔ akwadui ŋmɔŋ ko kɛjɛɔ tsɛnsi lɛ mli. Ekwɛɔ akwadui lɛ jogbaŋŋ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: The woman buys the bananas.
ga: Yoo lɛ heɔ akwadu lɛ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: More people come to the stall. They buy Tom's bananas and eat them.
ga: Mɛi babaoo baa shwapo lɛ mli. Amɛheɔ Tom akwadu ni amɛyeɔ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Soon, the tray is empty. Tom counts the money he earned.
ga: Etsɛɛɛ tsɔ, ni nɔ ko bɛ trati lɛ mli. Tom kaneɔ shika ni ená lɛ.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Then Tom buys soap, sugar, and bread. He puts the things in his tray.
ga: Kɛkɛ ni Tom he samla, sikli, kɛ aboloo. Ekɛ nibii lɛ woɔ etsɔne lɛ mli.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Tom balances the tray on his head and goes home.
ga: Tom kɛ trati ni yɔɔ eyitso nɔ lɛ toɔ he ni eyaa shia.
title: Tom the banana seller
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Humphreys Odunga, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Atilabachew Reda

english: Our special school
ga: Wɔ Skul Krɛdɛɛ lɛ
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: In a small village in Malawi, there was a special school. It was called Chiko, a short name for love.
ga: Yɛ Malawi akrowa bibioo ko mli lɛ, ayɛ skul krɛdɛɛ ko. Atsɛɔ lɛ Chiko, ni ji gbɛi kuku ni akɛtsɛɔ suɔmɔ.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: Our school was a place of hope and love. It was a school for orphans like me.
ga: Wɔ skul lɛ ji he ko ni hiɛnɔkamɔ kɛ suɔmɔ yɔɔ. Eji skul kɛha awusai tamɔ mi.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: Our school was surrounded by colourful flowers. There were bright reds, sunny yellows, and peaceful blues. Our school was a happy place.
ga: Fɔfɔi ni yɔɔ sui sɔrɔtoi ebɔle wɔ skul lɛ he fɛɛ. Ayɛ etsuru ni mli tse, hulutsoo ŋmɔŋ, kɛ toiŋjɔlɛ bluu. Wɔ skul lɛ ji he ko ni miishɛɛ yɔɔ.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: The staff gave us free food and school uniforms. It made us feel safe and loved.
ga: Nitsulɔi lɛ ha wɔ niyenii kɛ skul atadei ni apeee. Eha wɔnu he akɛ wɔyɛ shweshweeshwe ni asumɔ wɔ.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: Without this school, I would not have known how to read and write. I wouldn't have learned to add numbers or discover exciting stories in books.
ga: Eji skul nɛɛ bɛ kulɛ, mileee nikanemɔ kɛ niŋmaa. Kulɛ mikaseŋ bɔ ni akɛ yibɔi fataa he loo mana saji ni yɔɔ miishɛɛ yɛ woji amli.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: The teachers and staff at our school were like family. They made us feel important and cherished.
ga: Tsɔɔlɔi kɛ nitsulɔi ni yɔɔ wɔsukuu lɛ tamɔ weku. Amɛha wɔnu he akɛ wɔhe hiaa ni abuɔ wɔ waa.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: Every day at our school was a new adventure. We learned the value of helping others and being grateful for what we had.
ga: Gbi fɛɛ gbi yɛ wɔ skul lɛ ji nɔ ko hee ni wɔfeɔ. Wɔ kase sɛɛnamɔ ni yɔɔ mɛi krokomɛi ayebuamɔ kɛ shidaa ni wɔyɔɔ yɛ nɔ ni wɔyɔɔ lɛ he.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: My school taught me not only how to read and write but also how to be a better person. It showed me that with love, kindness, and education, we could overcome anything.
ga: Jeee nikanemɔ kɛ niŋmaa kɛkɛ ni miskul lɛ tsɔɔ mi, shi moŋ bɔ ni mafee gbɔmɔ kpakpa hu. Etsɔɔ mi akɛ kɛ wɔyɛ suɔmɔ, mlihilɛ, kɛ tsɔsemɔ lɛ, wɔbaanyɛ wɔye nɔ fɛɛ nɔ nɔ kunim.
title: Our special school
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Juwayiliya Bunaya, Zahira Suwedi, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Yankho Jere

english: We live in a skyscraper
ga: Wɔhiɔ ŋwɛitsu ko mli
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: People live in many different types of homes. Some people live in homes high in the sky. Others live in homes on the ground. Tall buildings can contain lots of homes that are built on top of each other. This book is about building a skyscraper with many floors.
ga: Gbɔmɛi hiɔ shiai sɔrɔtoi babaoo amli. Mɛi komɛi hiɔ shĩai ni yɔɔ ŋwɛi shɔɔŋ lɛ amli. Mɛi krokomɛi hu hiɔ tsũi ni yɔɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ lɛ amli. Tsuji ni kwɔlɔ baanyɛ afee nɔ ni tsũi babaoo ni ama yɛ amɛhe lɛ baanyɛ ahi mli. Wolo nɛɛ wieɔ ŋwɛi tsũ ko ni tsũi babaoo yɔɔ mli lɛ maa he.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Mishelle and Catherine are sisters. Mishelle has nearly finished high school. Catherine is in her final year of primary school. The sisters live with their parents and grandmother, in a tall building in Nairobi. They love to live high above the city, like birds in the tallest tree.
ga: Mishelle kɛ Catherine ji nyɛmimɛi yei. Shwɛ fioo ni Mishelle baagbe sukuu naa. Catherine yɛ enaagbee afi ni yɔɔ shishijee sukuu lɛ mli. Nyɛmimɛi yei lɛ kɛ amɛfɔlɔi kɛ amɛnaa hiɔ shi yɛ tsũ kwɔ ko mli yɛ Nairobi. Amɛsumɔɔ ni amɛhi maŋ lɛ nɔ shɔŋŋ, tamɔ okpoi ni yɔɔ tso ni kwɔ fe fɛɛ lɛ mli.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The family lives in an apartment on the 22nd floor of Tower Building. They use an elevator (or lift) to get to their home. Catherine counts floors as they travel up and down. She wants to be a pilot one day. Mishelle wants to be an engineer and build skyscrapers.
ga: Weku lɛ tsu ji yibɔi nyɔnmai enyɔ kɛ enyɔ (22) ni yɔɔ nwɛitsu lɛ mli. Amɛkɛ tsɔne ni kwɔɔ tsu (loo lifti) ni yaa amɛshia. Catherine kaneɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ be mli ni amɛyaa ŋwɛi kɛbaa shi lɛ. Esumɔɔ ni efee kɔɔyɔŋ lɛlɛ kudɔlɔ gbi ko. Mishelle sumɔ ni efee tsɔne he nilelɔ ni ema ŋwɛi tsũi wuji.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Catherine asks, "Is our building the tallest building in Africa?" Mishelle replies, "No, this building is about 126 meters tall. The tallest building in Africa is just over 393 meters. The tallest building in the world is nearly 830 meters!" "Wow! How do such tall buildings stay standing?" wonders Catherine.
ga: Catherine bi akɛ, "Ani wɔtsu lɛ ji tsu ni kwɔ fe fɛɛ yɛ Afrika?" Mishelle ha hetoo akɛ, "Daabi, nɛkɛ tsu nɛɛ kɛlɛ ji aaafee mitai oha kɛ nyɔŋmai enyɔ enumɔ (126). Tsu ni kwɔ fe fɛɛ yɛ Afrika lɛ fe mitai 393 fioo. Tsu ni kwɔ fe fɛɛ yɛ je lɛŋ lɛ miihe ashɛ mitai 830!" "Wow! Te efeɔ tɛŋŋ ni tsũi ni kwɔlɔ tamɔ nɛkɛ damɔ shi?" Catherine susuɔ he.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "Basically, all skyscrapers are made the same way. The two main building materials are steel and concrete. A skyscraper is built floor by floor, starting with a steel frame, and adding concrete around the frame. Those materials combined are extremely strong and last a long time," answers Mishelle.
ga: "Titri lɛ, afee ŋwɛi tsũi fɛɛ yɛ gbɛ kome nɔ. Tsumaa nibii titrii enyɔ lɛ ji dade kɛ kɔnkrit." Atswaa ŋwɛi tsũ ko shikpɔŋ kɛ shikpɔŋ, ni akɛ dade ŋtayaa jeɔ shishi, ni akɛ kɔnkrit woɔ ŋtayaa lɛ he. Nakai nibii ni akɛto he lɛ mli wa waa ni ehiɔ shi be kakadaŋŋ," Mishelle ha hetoo.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: To build a skyscraper, the construction workers must first dig a very deep pit for the building's foundation. In the same way that a tall tree has big, deep roots, a skyscraper must have a strong foundation on a layer of rock. Sometimes the rock is deep in the soil.
ga: Bɔni afee ni tsumaa nitsulɔi lɛ ama tsũ ko ni kwɔ waa lɛ, klɛŋklɛŋ lɛ, esa akɛ amɛtsa bu ko ni mli kwɔ waa kɛha tsũ lɛ shishitoo. Taakɛ bɔ ni tso kakadaŋŋ hiɛ shishifãi wuji ni mli kwɔ lɛ, nakai nɔŋŋ esa akɛ ŋwɛi tsũ ko hu aná shishitoo ni ma shi shiŋŋ yɛ tɛsaa ko nɔ. Bei komɛi lɛ, tɛsaa lɛ boteɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ mli shɔŋŋ.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Next, workers make a frame for the building. They build the frame with long pieces of steel. A framework of steel makes it possible to build a tall building. Steel can carry a lot of weight. A steel framework is the core of the building, like a person's skeleton.
ga: No sɛɛ lɛ, nitsulɔi feɔ tsu lɛ he mfoniri. Amɛkɛ dade kukuji kakadaji maa tsũ lɛ. Dade ni akɛfee tsɔne lɛ haa anyɛɔ amaa tsu ni kwɔ. Dade baanyɛ atere muji babaoo. Dade ni akɛfee tsũ lɛ ji nɔ titri ni yɔɔ tsu lɛ mli, tamɔ gbɔmɔ wu.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Steel can also be flexible. That means that a building can sway a little (although this is difficult to see). If there are extreme winds, or an earthquake, the internal steel structure lets a building sway slightly. Steel forms a core of flexible strength.
ga: Dade hu baanyɛ afee nɔ ni anyɛɔ atsakeɔ. No tsɔɔ akɛ tsu ko baanyɛ atswa fioo (eyɛ mli akɛ ewa akɛ aaana enɛ moŋ). Kɛji kɔɔyɔɔ ni naa wa, loo shikpɔŋhosomɔ ko ba lɛ, dade ni yɔɔ mli lɛ haa tsu ko shwieɔ shi fioo. Dade feɔ hewalɛ ni nyɛɔ etsakeɔ ehe lɛ shishitoo.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The other main building material is concrete. Concrete is a mix of materials like sand, cement, and water. Workers mix concrete to make a thick liquid, which they pour into frames around the steel structure. When concrete sets, it becomes solid, like rock. This makes the building's floors and walls.
ga: Tsumaa nibii titrii krokomɛi lɛ ji kɔnkrit. Kɔnkrit ji nibii tamɔ ŋã, simɛnti, kɛ nu ni akɛfutu mli. Nitsulɔi futuɔ kɔnkrit koni amɛfee nu ni mli edɔ, ni amɛshwieɔ amɛwoɔ fremji ni bɔleɔ dade tsũ lɛ he lɛ amli. Kɛ́ kɔnkrit lɛ shwie shi lɛ, ebafeɔ nɔ ni wa, tamɔ tɛ. Enɛ haa tsu lɛ shikpɔŋ kɛ gbogboi feɔ.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Workers build a skyscraper upwards, floor by floor. Lower floors must support a lot of weight. Concrete can support that pressure, making the building strong and stable. The concrete is a layer around the steel framework, protecting the metal from water and air. (Water and air cause metal to rust.)
ga: Nitsulɔi ma ŋwɛi tsũ ko kɛyaa ŋwɛi, shikpɔŋ kɛ shikpɔŋ. Esa akɛ shishigbɛ tsũi lɛ aŋmɛ muji babaoo sɛɛ. Kɔnkrit baanyɛ afi nakai nɔnyɛɛ lɛ sɛɛ, ni eha tsu lɛ mli awa ni ehi shi shiŋŋ. Kɔnkrit lɛ ji nɔ ko ni bɔleɔ dade lɛ he, ni ebuɔ dade lɛ he kɛjɛɔ nu kɛ kɔɔyɔɔ he. (Nu kɛ kɔɔyɔɔ haa dade shwieɔ shi.)
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: The shafts for the lifts are also built during this stage. When the steel and concrete structure is complete, workers install windows. Then they add ceilings and walls and complete the floors. The building needs electrical wiring and a network of pipes for water and sanitation.
ga: Atswaa tsɔnei ni akɛwoɔ tsɔne mli lɛ hu yɛ nɛkɛ be nɛɛ mli. Kɛ́ agbe dade kɛ kɔnkrit tsũ lɛ naa lɛ, nitsulɔi lɛ kɛ samfɛji woɔ mli. Kɛkɛ lɛ, amɛkɛ ŋwɛitsu kɛ gbogboi fataa he ni amɛgbeɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ. Tsu lɛ he miihia ni akɛ srawa hewalɛ awo mli kɛ paipii ni akɛwoɔ nu kɛ hetsemɔ mli.
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Finally, workers put in lights, doors, cupboards, and other things for living and working in a skyscraper. Mishelle says, "Many big cities are running out of space. Tall buildings make good use of space. When I'm an engineer, I'll help to build the tallest skyscraper on earth!"
ga: Yɛ naagbee lɛ, nitsulɔi lɛ kɛ kanei, shinaai, adekai, kɛ nibii krokomɛi ni akɛhiɔ shi kɛ nitsumɔ woɔ tsũ ko ni kwɔ waa mli. Mishelle kɛɛ, "Maji wuji babaoo amli he ko miiho. Tsuji ni kwɔlɔ kɛ he ko tsuɔ nii jogbaŋŋ. Kɛ́ miji tsɔne he nilelɔ lɛ, maye mabua ni ama ŋwɛi tsũ ni kwɔ fe fɛɛ yɛ shikpɔŋ nɔ!"
title: We live in a skyscraper
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: We live in a manyatta
ga: Wɔhiɔ sũ tsũ mli
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: People live in many different types of homes. Some people live in homes that are built to last a long time. Others live in homes that are temporary and don't last long. This book is about a temporary homestead called a manyatta, which is made up of traditional huts.
ga: Gbɔmɛi hiɔ shiai sɔrɔtoi babaoo amli. Mɛi komɛi hiɔ shĩai ni amamɔ koni amɛhi shi be kakadaŋŋ lɛ amli. Mɛi krokomɛi hu hiɔ shĩai ni hiɔ shi yɛ be kukuoo mli, ni ehiii shi be kakadaŋŋ lɛ amli. Wolo nɛɛ wieɔ be kukuoo mli shia ko ni atsɛɔ lɛ sũ tsũ, ni blema tsũi fee lɛ he.
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: This manyatta is in north-central Kenya, in Samburu County. Sisters Sidai and Naeku share a hut, and their parents and baby brother share a hut. Their uncle and three older brothers stay in the other huts, along with their families.
ga: Nɛkɛ sũ tsũ nɛɛ yɛ Kenya kooyi-teŋgbɛ, yɛ Samburu Maŋ lɛ mli. Ayɛ tsũi nyɔŋma ni abua fɛɛ naa. Nyɛmimɛi yei Sidai kɛ Naeku hiɔ tsũ kome mli, ni amɛfɔlɔi kɛ amɛnyɛmi nuu bibioo lɛ hu hiɔ tsũ kome mli. Amɛtsɛkwɛ kɛ amɛnyɛmimɛi hii onukpai etɛ hiɔ tsũi krokomɛi lɛ amli, kɛ amɛwekui.
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: The families graze their cattle together and help each other. They don't stay in one place for very long. They move to find new grazing areas for the cattle. Around the manyatta is a fence of thorn branches. This fence keeps in the cattle and keeps out strangers.
ga: Wekui lɛ feɔ ekome kɛyeɔ amɛtsinai lɛ ni amɛyeɔ amɛbuaa amɛhe. Amɛhiɛɛɛ he kome be kakadaŋŋ. Amɛfãa koni amɛyatao hei heei ni tsinai lɛ yeɔ niyenii yɛ. Akɛ ŋmeii niji ebɔle sũ tsũ lɛ he. Nɛkɛ gbogbo nɛɛ haa tsinai lɛ hiɔ shi ni ehaaa gbɔi akabote mli.
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "We begin the building process by collecting materials from our environment. We gather tree branches to build the basic structure of the hut," says Sidai. Naeku adds, "We know how to use natural materials to create our homes. Everyone in the manyatta helps with building."
ga: Sidai kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔjeɔ tsumaa nitsumɔ lɛ shishi kɛtsɔ nibii ni wɔbuaa naa kɛjɛɔ wɔshihilɛhe lɛ nɔ. Wɔbuaa tsei niji anaa koni wɔkɛma tsũ lɛ shishijee shishitoo lɛ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔle bɔ ni akɛ adebɔɔ mli nibii tsuɔ nii kɛfeɔ wɔshiai. Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ ni yɔɔ manyatta lɛ yeɔ ebuaa kɛ tsumaa."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "We use bigger branches to make a strong frame for the walls. We tie the roof frame to the wall frame with climbers, making a sturdy frame for the whole hut," explains Sidai. "The huts have low roofs, making it harder for the wind to blow them over," adds Naeku.
ga: Sidai tsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Wɔkɛ tsei niji wuji tsuɔ nii kɛfeɔ gbogboi lɛ ahe tsɔne ni wa. Wɔkɛ mɛi ni kwɔɔ gɔŋ lɛ fĩɔ tsũ lɛ yiteŋ tsɔne lɛ he, ni wɔfeɔ tsɔne ni wa kɛhaa tsũ muu lɛ fɛɛ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Tsũi lɛ ayiteŋ baa shi, ni no haa ewaa kɛhaa kɔɔyɔɔ lɛ akɛ ebaatswa amɛ."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Sidai continues, "Once the frame of the hut is standing, we weave thin branches in between the thicker branches." Naeku adds, "We create thick layers of grass and tie them on to the roof frame. This is called thatching." "Good thatching protects us from rain and sun," adds Sidai.
ga: Sidai tsa nɔ akɛ, "Kɛ tsũ lɛ damɔ shi lɛ, wɔkpɛɔ niji bibii yɛ niji ni tsii lɛ ateŋ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔfeɔ jwɛi ni mli tse ni wɔkɛkpɛtɛɔ tsũ lɛ yiteŋ. Atsɛɔ enɛ akɛ jwɛi ni akɛwoɔ tsũ lɛ mli." Sidai kɛfata he akɛ, "Jwɛi kpakpai buɔ wɔhe kɛjɛɔ nugbɔ kɛ hulu he."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Sidai adds, "The roofs of our huts can be flat or round." Naeku says, "Plastering is my favourite part of building. We mix mud and dung to make a natural plaster. We pack this plaster into the wall frame, filling the spaces. This helps to keep out wind and sand."
ga: Sidai kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔ tsũi lɛ ayiteŋ baanyɛ afee ŋmɔlɔŋmɔlɔ loo kokroo." Naeku kɛɛ, "Gbogbo he plasta ji nɔ ni misumɔɔ waa yɛ tsumaa mli. Wɔfutuɔ sũ kɛ sũ ni wɔkɛfeɔ plasta. Wɔkɛ plasta nɛɛ woɔ gbogbo lɛ mli, ni wɔwoɔ hei ni etse lɛ amli. Enɛ yeɔ ebuaa ni kɔɔyɔɔ kɛ ŋã baa."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: Sidai continues, "Packing plaster into the walls seals them once those walls are dry. We also plaster the surface of the walls. Dried plaster is hard and strong." Naeku adds, "There are no windows in the walls, but our hut has a wooden door."
ga: Sidai tsa nɔ akɛ, "Plasta ni akɛwoɔ gbogboi lɛ amli lɛ haa amɛtsiɔ amɛhe kɛji nakai gbogboi lɛ egbi. Wɔkɛ plasta woɔ gbogboi lɛ anɔ hu. Plasta ni egbi lɛ wa ni eyɛ hewalɛ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Samfɛji bɛ gbogboi lɛ amli, shi wɔ tsũ lɛ yɛ tso shinaa."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "Plastering the walls insulates the hut," says Sidai. "What does 'insulate' mean?" asks Naeku. "Mud and dung walls help to keep the hut cool inside when it's hot outside. In cooler weather, the walls help to keep us warm inside by holding in the fire's heat," replies her sister.
ga: Sidai kɛɛ akɛ, "Plasta ni akɛwoɔ gbogboi lɛ ahe lɛ haa shĩa lɛ mli tseɔ." "Mɛni ji 'tsu lɛ mli jɔɔ ŋanii' shishi?" Naeku biɔ. "Mu kɛ sũ mli gbogboi yeɔ ebuaa ni ehaa tsũ lɛ mli feɔ fɛ̃i yɛ kpo nɔ. Yɛ be mli ni hulutsoo be lɛ mli lɛ, gbogboi lɛ yeɔ ebuaa ni ehaa wɔhe feɔ fɛ̃i yɛ mli kɛtsɔ la lɛ mli dɔlɛ ni amɛhiɛɔ mli lɛ nɔ," enyɛmi yoo lɛ haa hetoo.
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "Everyone in the manyatta helps to build, and we all help to take apart the huts when we move. It's not difficult to take apart the structures and use the parts again in a new place," Sidai explains.
ga: "Mɔ fɛɛ mɔ ni yɔɔ sũ tsũ mli lɛ yeɔ ebuaa kɛmaa, ni wɔ fɛɛ wɔyeɔ wɔbuaa kɛjieɔ tsũi lɛ amli kɛji wɔfã." Sidai tsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Ewaaa akɛ aaatse tsɔnei ni akɛfee lɛ amli ni akɛ fãi lɛ atsu nii ekoŋŋ yɛ he hee."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "Our building materials are light, so it is easy to transport them. We use camels or donkeys to carry any useful materials from our old manyatta. For example, the thatched roof," says Sidai. "We can also collect more building materials from the environment in the new place," adds Naeku.
ga: Sidai kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔ tsumaa he nibii lɛ waaa, no hewɔ lɛ, ewaaa akɛ wɔkɛbaatsu nii. Wɔkɛ afukpɔŋɔi loo tejii tsuɔ nii kɛwoɔ nibii fɛɛ ni he yɔɔ sɛɛnamɔ ni jɛ wɔ sũ tsũ momo lɛ mli lɛ. Akɛ nɔkwɛmɔnɔ lɛ, tsũ lɛ yiteŋ ni akɛ jwɛi fee lɛ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔbaanyɛ wɔbua tsumaa he nibii babaoo hu anaa kɛjɛ shihilɛ ni yɔɔ he hee lɛ mli lɛ mli."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: "Our home suits the way that we live, which is to move around with our herds," says Sidai. "Moving around means we can't always go to school with our friends," says Naeku. "Our school lets us borrow books, and we try to keep up with schoolwork," adds Sidai.
ga: Sidai kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔshia lɛ sa gbɛ ni wɔtsɔɔ nɔ wɔhiɔ shi lɛ nɔ, ni ji ni wɔkɛ wɔtooi lɛ aya he fɛɛ he." Naeku kɛɛ akɛ, "Kɛ wɔfã kɛya he kroko lɛ, no tsɔɔ akɛ wɔnyɛŋ wɔkɛ wɔnanemɛi aya sukuu be fɛɛ be." Sidai kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔ sukuu lɛ haa wɔfaa woji, ni wɔbɔɔ mɔdɛŋ ni wɔtsu sukuu nitsumɔi lɛ ahe nii."
title: We live in a manyatta
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Arthur Makali

english: We live in a nest
ga: Wɔhiɔ shi yɛ loofɔlɔ tsu mli
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Insects live in many different types of homes. Some insects live together in large groups, some live alone. This storybook is about Naeku and Naserian - two sister termites living in the grasslands of southern Kenya. The sisters live in a colony with about 80,000 other termites.
ga: Kplukai hiɔ shiai srɔtoi babaoo amli. Kooloi bibii komɛi feɔ ekome kɛhiɔ shi yɛ kui wuji amli, ekomɛi hu hiɔ shi amɛkomekomei. Nɛkɛ sane nɛɛ kɔɔ Naeku kɛ Naserian - nyɛmimɛi yei enyɔ ni ji nmei ni hiɔ jwɛi shikpɔji ni yɔɔ Kenya kooyigbɛ lɛ anɔ lɛ ahe. Nyɛmimɛi yei lɛ hiɔ he ko ni ŋmeii krokomɛi aaafee 80,000 yɔɔ mli.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Termites are social insects living in a large group. They have different roles for creating and maintaining the colony. Worker termites like Naserian and Naeku dig and build the nest. Soldier termites guard the nest. Both workers and soldiers go out to find new places to build nests.
ga: Ŋmei kuu ko hiɔ shĩa ko ni akɛ shikpɔŋ fee lɛ mli. Nɛkɛ ŋmei nɛɛ baanyɛ ahi shikpɔŋ shishi, loo shikpɔŋ yiteŋ, loo fɛɛ. Fã ni wɔbaanyɛ wɔna yɛ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ lɛ ji ŋmeii akutso. Ŋmei gɔji lɛ ateŋ babaoo yɛ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ aaafee mitai enyɔ kɛyashi enumɔ.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Termites in the colony do different activities for the whole group. Naeku and Naserian are worker termites. All workers are female. "We are the builders and engineers!" says Naeku. The worker termites build and maintain the termite nest. Naserian says, "We build large, complex structures."
ga: Ŋmeii ni yɔɔ ŋshɔ lɛ mli lɛ feɔ nibii srɔtoi amɛhaa kuu muu lɛ fɛɛ. Naeku kɛ Naserian ji nitsulɔi ŋmeii. Nitsulɔi lɛ fɛɛ ji yei. "Wɔ ji tsumalɔi kɛ tsɔne he nilelɔi!" Naeku kɛɛ. Nitsulɔi ŋmeii lɛ maa ŋmeii lɛ atsu lɛ ni amɛkwɛɔ nɔ. Naserian kɛɛ, "Wɔmaa tsũi wuji ni mli wa."
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "Let's explain how we build our homes," suggests Naeku. "We begin by digging underground tunnels through the earth." Naserian interrupts, "We use our powerful jaws to dig through the earth. We can move a lot of soil!"
ga: Naeku wo ŋaa akɛ, "Nyɛhaa wɔtsɔɔa bɔ ni wɔmaa wɔshiai lɛ mli. Wɔjeɔ shishi kɛ shikpɔŋ shishi gbɛjegbɛi ni wɔfoɔ kɛtsɔɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ lɛ." Naserian kpa ewiemɔ lɛ mli akɛ, "Wɔkɛ wɔtsitsii ni yɔɔ hewalɛ lɛ tsuɔ nii kɛfoɔ shikpɔŋ lɛ mli. Wɔbaanyɛ wɔtsi shikpɔŋ babaoo!"
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "To make sure that the walls of our tunnels are strong, we cover them with a sticky mixture of spit (saliva) and soil," says Naserian. "When the sticky mixture dries, it becomes hard like clay. Termite nests can last a very long time," adds Naeku.
ga: Naserian kɛɛ akɛ, "Bɔni afee ni wɔkwɛ akɛ wɔ ŋshɔkei lɛ agbogboi lɛ mli wa lɛ, wɔkɛ ŋmɔtɔ (ŋmei) kɛ sũ ni akɛfutuɔ nii ni mli tseɔ haa amɛhe." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Kɛ́ ŋmɔtɔ ni akɛfutuɔ nii lɛ gĩ lɛ, ebafeɔ nɔ ni wa tamɔ shikpɔŋ. Ŋmei shĩai baanyɛ ahi shi be kakadaŋŋ waa."
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "We carry out the soil that we dig and use it to build a mound above the ground. The mound is usually round or a cone shape, with many tunnels," says Naserian. "Some termite mounds are as high as nine meters!" says Naeku.
ga: Naserian kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔtsuɔ shikpɔŋ ni wɔfoɔ lɛ he nii ni wɔkɛtsuɔ nii kɛmaa gɔŋ ko yɛ shikpɔŋ lɛ nɔ. Bei pii lɛ, gɔŋ lɛ feɔ kokroo loo efeɔ tamɔ kɔne, ni gbɛjegbɛi babaoo yɔɔ mli." "Ŋmei gɔji komɛi anɔ kwɔ fe mitai nɛɛhu!" Naeku kɛɛ.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Termites are social insects living in a large group. They have different roles for creating and maintaining the colony. Worker termites like Naserian and Naeku dig and build the nest. Soldier termites guard the nest. Both workers and soldiers go out to find new places to build nests.
ga: Ŋmei ji kooloi ni hiɔ shi yɛ kuu agbo mli. Amɛyɛ nitsumɔi srɔtoi kɛha maŋ lɛ shishitoo kɛ ekwɛmɔ. Nitsulɔi ŋmeii tamɔ Naserian kɛ Naeku lɛ shwieɔ ŋmeii lɛ ni amɛmaa ŋmeii lɛ. Asraafoi a-termites buɔ ŋshɔŋlooi lɛ ahe. Nitsulɔi kɛ asraafoi fɛɛ jeɔ kpo koni amɛyatao hei heei ni amɛyamamɔ amɛtsui yɛ.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Nurse termites look after the queen and baby termites called larvae. The nest has different areas. There are rooms for the queen, rooms for the larvae, and rooms for storing food. Tunnels link the different areas. The queen is the biggest termite and can live the longest.
ga: Nɛsifonyo ŋmei kwɛɔ maŋnyɛ kɛ ŋmeii bibii ni atsɛɔ amɛhu ŋmei lɛ anɔ. Hei srɔtoi yɛ ŋshɔŋloo lɛ mli. Ayɛ tsũi kɛha maŋnyɛ lɛ, tsũi kɛha ŋmeii, kɛ tsũi ni akɛ niyenii toɔ. Gbɛjegbɛi lɛ kɛ hei srɔtoi lɛ tsaa. Maŋnyɛ lɛ ji ŋmei ni da fe fɛɛ ni ebaanyɛ ehi shi be kakadaŋŋ fe fɛɛ.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Naserian continues, "We build tunnels or shafts out to the surface for fresh air to flow through the nest." Naeku adds, "Termites need fresh air to live." Naserian explains, "The shafts also help to control the temperature in the nest so that it doesn't get too hot."
ga: Naserian tsa nɔ akɛ, "Wɔmaa gbɛjegbɛi loo ŋshɔkei kɛyaa ŋshɔ lɛ hiɛ koni kɔɔyɔɔ kpakpa atsɔ ŋshɔ lɛ mli." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Kɔɔyɔɔ kpakpa he miihia ŋmeii koni amɛhi shi." Naserian tsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Shaftii lɛ hu yeɔ ebuaa ni ekwɛɔ hulutsoo ni yɔɔ ŋshɔ lɛ mli lɛ nɔ koni edɔ tsɔ."
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: "We have gardens in our nest, where we grow fungus. We collect tiny bits of plants and other natural materials, which we use to grow fungus," says Naserian. "Yum!" exclaims Naeku. "The fungus gardens feed the whole colony. We are the only type of termite that farms fungus."
ga: Naserian kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔyɛ abɔɔi yɛ wɔtsu lɛ mli, he ni wɔduɔ ŋmeii yɛ. Wɔbuaa tsei bibii kɛ adebɔɔ mli nibii krokomɛi anaa, ni wɔkɛduɔ nii." "Yum!" Naeku bolɔ. "Ŋmeii abɔɔi lɛ yeɔ koloni muu lɛ fɛɛ. Wɔ pɛ ji ŋmeii ni tsuɔ ŋmei ahe nii."
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Termite colonies have a queen and king. The workers feed and protect these important members of the colony. A queen termite usually lives about 20 to 30 years. She can lay millions of eggs in her lifetime. Larvae hatch from eggs and nurse termites care for them.
ga: Ŋmei akutsei lɛ yɛ maŋnyɛ kɛ maŋtsɛ. Nitsulɔi lɛ haa nɛkɛ maŋ lɛ mli bii ni he hiaa nɛɛ niyenii ni amɛbuɔ amɛhe. Bei pii lɛ, maŋnyɛ ŋmei hiɔ shi aaafee afii 20 kɛyashi 30. Ebaanyɛ efɔ ŋmeii akpekpei abɔ yɛ ewala beaŋ. ŋmei lɛ fɔɔ kɛjɛɔ amɛwɔji amli ni ŋmeii ni kwɛɔ amɛ nɔ lɛ kwɛɔ amɛ.
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: Naserian says, "Termite society is very well organised. Every termite contributes to the survival and growth of the whole colony." Naeku adds, "We each have a job to do, and we do it. Termites work well together." "Yes," agrees Naserian. "Now let's get back to digging!"
ga: Naserian kɛɛ, "Ato ŋmeii akuu lɛ he gbɛjianɔ jogbaŋŋ. Ŋmeii fɛɛ ŋmeii yeɔ ebuaa ŋmeii akuu muu lɛ fɛɛ wala kɛ dalɛ." Naeku kɛfata he akɛ, "Wɔteŋ mɔ fɛɛ mɔ yɛ nitsumɔ ni etsuɔ, ni wɔtsuɔ. Ŋmei tsuɔ nii jogbaŋŋ." Naserian kpɛlɛɔ nɔ akɛ, "Hɛɛ. Agbɛnɛ nyɛhaa wɔkuɔ wɔsɛɛ wɔyaa shitsamɔ nɔ!"
title: We live in a nest
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Kenneth Boyowa Okitikpi

english: We live in a rondavel
ga: Wɔhiɔ su tsu kokloo ko mli
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: People live in many different types of homes. Some homes are built with natural materials, such as grass. Other homes are built with human-made materials, such as glass and concrete. Some homes are built with both natural and manufactured materials, like the rondavel in this story.
ga: Gbɔmɛi hiɔ shiai sɔrɔtoi babaoo amli. Akɛ adebɔɔ mli nibii tamɔ jwɛi maa tsũi komɛi. Akɛ nibii ni adesai fee, tamɔ glase kɛ kɔnkrit maa tsũi krokomɛi. Akɛ adebɔɔ mli nibii kɛ nibii ni afee lɛ fɛɛ maa tsũi komɛi, tamɔ su tsu kokloo ni yɔɔ sane nɛɛ mli lɛ.
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Kabo and Thabo live in the Kgatleng District of Botswana, near the village of Mochudi. They live in a rondavel with their parents. "A rondavel is a traditional round house with a thatched roof. These homes are built in many parts of southern Africa," explains Kabo.
ga: Kabo kɛ Thabo yɛ Botswana Kgatleng Kpokpaa lɛ nɔ, yɛ Mochudi akrowa lɛ masɛi. Amɛkɛ amɛfɔlɔi hiɔ su tsu kokloo ko mli. Kabo tsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Su tsu kokloo ji kusum tsũ ko ni yɔɔ kokroo ni jwɛi eyiteŋ. Atswa tsũi nɛɛ yɛ Afrika kooyigbɛ hei babaoo."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Thabo continues, "Most rondavels are round, with a door and windows. We have glass windows, which they didn't have in the old days." "Our grandfather built this rondavel in the traditional way. Our father added some modern materials," says Kabo.
ga: Thabo tsa nɔ akɛ, "Su tsu kokloo lɛ ateŋ babaoo ji kokroo, ni amɛyɛ shinaa kɛ samfɛji. Wɔyɛ glase samfɛji, ni amɛbɛ yɛ blema beaŋ." Kabo kɛɛ akɛ, "Wɔtsɛkwɛ̃ ma su tsu kokloo nɛɛ yɛ kusum gbɛ nɔ. Wɔtsɛ kɛ ŋmɛnɛŋmɛnɛ beaŋ nibii komɛi fata he."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: "Let's explain the building process," suggests Kabo. He says, "The builders used timber, thatch, stones, mortar and plaster. They began by digging a pit. They packed the pit with small stones, soil, and sand. This made a firm and strong foundation to build on."
ga: Kabo wo ŋaa akɛ, "Nyɛhaa wɔtsɔɔ bɔ ni amaa tsu lɛ ahaa lɛ mli. Tsumalɔi lɛ kɛ tsei, jwɛi, tɛi, sũ kɛ plɔta tsu nii. Amɛje shishi kɛtsɔ bu ko ni amɛtsa lɛ nɔ. Amɛkɛ tɛi bibii, sũ, kɛ ŋã eyi bu lɛ mli obɔ. Enɛ fee shishitoo ni ma shi shiŋŋ ni akɛma nɔ."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Thabo continues, "The builders pushed long wooden poles into the foundation, around the outer edge. They tied the poles together, making a wooden frame for the outside walls. Once the basic structure was finished, the builders put stones closely together in the frame."
ga: Thabo tsa nɔ akɛ, "Tsumalɔi lɛ tsi tsei kakadaji amɛwo shishitoo lɛ mli, ni amɛbɔle kponɔgbɛ naa. Amɛfimɔ tsei lɛ ahe, ni amɛfee tso ni akɛfee kponɔgbɛ gbogboi lɛ." Beni agbe tsũ lɛ naa lɛ, tsumalɔi lɛ kɛ tɛi bɛŋkɛ amɛhe yɛ frem lɛ mli."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: "Next, the builders mixed clay, water, and cow dung. This makes a natural mortar that is extremely hard when dry. They packed the mortar between the stones to fix them in place," says Kabo. "Building with stones and mortar makes strong walls that last a long time," adds Thabo.
ga: Kabo kɛɛ akɛ, "Nɔ ni nyiɛ sɛɛ ji akɛ, tsumalɔi lɛ kɛ shikpɔŋ, nu, kɛ tsina ŋmɔtɔ futu mli. Enɛ feɔ adebɔɔ mli sũ ni wa waa kɛji egbi. Amɛwo sũ lɛ mli yɛ tɛi lɛ ateŋ koni amɛkɛsaa amɛ jogbaŋŋ." Thabo kɛfata he akɛ, "Tɛi kɛ sũ ni akɛtswaa tsu lɛ haa gbogboi ni wa ni hiɔ shi be kakadaŋŋ lɛ feɔ."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Kabo says, "The thick outer walls insulate our rondavel." Thabo explains, "Insulation means that it stays cool inside when the weather is hot outside. The sun's heat can't get through the walls. In places with cold winters, this insulation keeps rondavels warm in winter by keeping the heat inside."
ga: Kabo kɛɛ, "Kponɔgbɛ gbogboi ni mli tse lɛ tsiɔ wɔ su tsu kokloo lɛ naa." Thabo tsɔɔ mli akɛ, "Tsu lɛ mli jɔɔ ŋanii kɛji kpo nɔ edɔ. Hulu la ni tsoɔ lɛ nyɛɛ atsɔ gbogboi lɛ amli." "Yɛ hei ni fɛ̃i be yɔɔ lɛ, nɛkɛ tsɔne nɛɛ haa su tsu kokloo lɛ mli dɔɔ yɛ fɛ̃i be mli kɛtsɔ dɔlɛ ni eyɔɔ mli lɛ nɔ."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: "Builders created the floor of our rondavel by packing mud into the foundation they made," says Thabo. Kabo says, "To complete the floor, they spread a final layer of mud and packed it down. This dried hard and created a flat, even surface for the floor."
ga: Thabo kɛɛ akɛ, "Tsumalɔi fee wɔ su tsu kokloo lɛ shikpɔŋ kɛtsɔ sũ ni amɛkɛwo shishitoo ni amɛfee lɛ mli lɛ nɔ." Kabo kɛɛ, "Koni amɛgbe shikpɔŋ lɛ naa lɛ, amɛgbɛ sũ naagbee fã ko amɛshwã ni amɛwo mli. Enɛ gĩ waa ni eha shikpɔŋ lɛ fee ŋmɔlɔŋmɔlɔ."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Thabo says, "The last stage was putting on the roof. Rondavels usually have a pointed thatch roof. Builders made a wooden frame with poles joined together in a point in the middle. They sewed bundles of thatch grasses to the poles in layers. A thatch roof is waterproof."
ga: Thabo kɛɛ, "Naagbee gbɛ lɛ ji ni akɛ tsũ lɛ yiteŋ awo. Bei pii lɛ, su tsu kokloo lɛ yɛ tsũ lɛ yiteŋ ni akɛ jwɛi fee ni yɔɔ ŋmɔlɔŋmɔlɔ." Tsumalɔi fee tso ni akɛ tsei ebɔ he yɛ he ko yɛ teŋgbɛ. Amɛkpɛɔ jwɛi ni akɛfee tsũ lɛ mli lɛ ŋmɔlɔŋmɔlɔ kɛkpɛtɛ tsei lɛ ahe. Jwɛi tsũ yiteŋ nyɛɛɛ nu abote mli."
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Thatch is a useful material for a roof. But this natural material also makes a good home for insects and other animals. Many of them are pests! Look at the picture and find: three spiders, a scorpion, a beetle, a termite, and a mouse?
ga: Jwɛi ji nɔ ko ni he hiaa waa kɛha tsũ yiteŋ. Shi nɛkɛ adebɔɔ mli nibii nɛɛ hu feɔ shia kpakpa kɛha kooloi bibii kɛ kooloi krokomɛi. Amɛteŋ mɛi babaoo ji kooloi! Kwɛmɔ mfoniri lɛ ni ona: anaanu etɛ, ŋmeii, kɛ kwakwe?
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Natural materials such as thatch grass create a good environment for spiders to live and hunt. Spiders don't damage the thatch and they help to control other insects. We need to look after the thatch to keep out pests such as mice, fleas, and termites.
ga: Adebɔɔ mli nibii tamɔ jwɛi ni yɔɔ ŋwɛi lɛ haa shihilɛ kpakpa baa anaanui ni amɛhiɔ shi ni amɛyataoɔ. Anaanui fiteee jwɛi lɛ ni amɛyeɔ amɛbuaa ni amɛyeɔ kooloi krokomɛi anɔ. Esa akɛ wɔkwɛ jwɛi lɛ nɔ jogbaŋŋ koni kooloi tamɔ kwakwei, kɛ ŋmeii akabote mli.
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: "There are a lot of us living in this rondavel!" says Thabo, looking at the thatch. He is afraid of spiders. "I wonder what other creatures live around us?" asks Kabo, nervously. "When I build my home, I will build a rondavel with a tiled roof!" laughs Kabo.
ga: "Wɔteŋ mɛi babaoo yɛ su tsu kokloo nɛɛ mli!" Thabo kɛɛ, ni ekwɛɔ jwɛi lɛ. Esheɔ anaanui gbeyei. "Misusuɔ akɛ mɛɛ bɔɔ nii krokomɛi hiɔ shi yɛ wɔhe?" Kabo biɔ, kɛ gbeyeishemɔ. "Kɛ́ mima mishia lɛ, matswa su tsu kokloo ni akɛ tile ewo ŋwɛitsu lɛ nɔ!" Kabo ŋmɔɔ.
title: We live in a rondavel
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Nina Orange, Ursula Nafula, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vusi Malindi

english: Our home, your home
ga: Wɔshia, oshia
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: Terna was a homeless man. He sought fruits for food in the forest. He sometimes slept there as baboons and gorillas watched him from the trees and bushes.
ga: Terna ji nuu ko ni bɛ shia. Etao aduawai kɛha niyenii yɛ koo lɛ mli. Bei komɛi lɛ, ewɔɔ jɛmɛ beni ŋmeii kɛ Adun Akaai kwɛɔ lɛ kɛjɛɔ tsei kɛ jwɛi amli lɛ.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: He wandered through the forest and saw more and more trees. "These trees are here wasting away," he imagined.
ga: Etsɔ koo lɛ mli ni ena tsei babaoo. "Tsei nɛɛ yɛ biɛ ni amɛmiifite," esusu he.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: Tired of wandering, he sat down, leaned on one of the trees and slept. The trees sheltered him from the sun and the birds flew above singing sweet songs.
ga: Akɛni etɔ lɛ akɛ ebaafã gbɛ hewɔ lɛ, eta shi, ekɛ ehe fɔ̃ɔ tsei lɛ eko nɔ ni ewɔ. Tsei lɛ bu ehe kɛjɛ hulu lɛ he ni okpoi lɛ foɔ kɛyaa ŋwɛi ni amɛlaa lalai ni ŋɔɔ.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: He had an idea. "If I cut down some trees, I could make money and become an owner of many mansions."
ga: Ena susumɔ ko. "Kɛ mifo tsei komɛi lɛ, manyɛ maná shika ni matsɔ tsũi wuji babaoo nuŋtsɔ."
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: He went to the village and borrowed a saw. He started cutting down trees. The gorilla begged him, "Please, don't cut down the trees. They are home for us and the birds. Their fruits are our food."
ga: Etee akrowa lɛ mli ni eyafa tsɔne ni akɛfoɔ tsei. Ebɔi tsei lɛ folɔmɔ. Adun Akaa lɛ kpa lɛ fai akɛ, "Ofainɛ, kaafo tsei lɛ. Amɛji shia kɛha wɔ kɛ okpoi lɛ. Amɛyibii ji wɔ niyenii."
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: "I need money to make my own home," Terna said. "It is selfish for you to destroy the home of many animals and birds to make yours," the gorilla said. Terna was sorry. He dropped the saw and hugged the gorilla.
ga: Terna kɛɛ akɛ, "Shika he miihia mi koni mafee mi diɛŋtsɛ mishia." Adun Akaa lɛ kɛɛ akɛ, "Eji pɛsɛmkunya akɛ obaafite kooloi kɛ okpoi babaoo ashia koni ofee onɔ̃." Edɔ Terna. Ekɛ tsɔne ni akɛfoɔ tsei lɛ shwie shi ni efua Adun Akaa lɛ.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: His friend, the gorilla suggested that he could use mud to make bricks. Then use grass and dead wood to make the hut. That way, both of them could have homes.
ga: Enaanyo, Adun Akaa lɛ wo ŋaa akɛ ebaanyɛ ekɛ sũ afee brikii ni ekɛ jwɛi kɛ tsei ni egboi afee tsũ lɛ. Nakai lɛ, amɛyi enyɔ lɛ fɛɛ amɛbaanyɛ amɛná shĩai.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule

english: Terna agreed. He visited the gorilla often. The gorilla allowed him to pluck as many fruits and dead wood as he could. They became very good friends.
ga: Terna kpɛlɛ nɔ. Eyasaraa Adun Akaa lɛ shii abɔ. Adun Akaa lɛ ha efolɔ aduawai kɛ tsei ni egboi babaoo bɔ ni eeenyɛ. Amɛbatsɔmɔ nanemɛi kpakpai waa.
title: Our home, your home
source: African Storybook Initiative, africanstorybook.org (Attribution 4.0) — story by Vyandeh Terkule, Ga translation by Evans Korletey-Tene, illustrations by Vyandeh Terkule
